name: SBIR/STTR Phase I at a grant agency (NIH, NSF, DOE, USDA, NIST, NOAA)
governing_text: 15 U.S.C. 638; SBA SBIR/STTR Policy Directive (May 3, 2023); Pub. L. 119-83
what: A small firm with its own technology applies for a [Phase I](#term:phase-i) award from an agency that funds [SBIR](#term:sbir)/[STTR](#term:sttr) as [grants](#term:grant) or cooperative agreements, under that agency's own [notice of funding opportunity](#term:nofo) [3](#cite:3) [5](#cite:5) [12](#cite:12). The firm must have not more than 500 employees with [affiliates](#term:affiliation) and be more than 50 percent owned by U.S. citizens or permanent residents, and it registers with SBA's [company registry](#term:sbir-gov) before applying [10](#cite:10) [5](#cite:5). As of April 2026 agencies may award up to $323,090 for Phase I without SBA approval [11](#cite:11).
who_for: A firm with a technology at the research or feasibility stage; the PI must be primarily employed by the firm for SBIR, and for STTR a research institution does at least 30 percent of the work [5](#cite:5).
how_it_works: Find the agency's current notice: [NIH](#term:agency-abbreviations) parent notices PA-27-100 (SBIR) and PA-27-102 (STTR) with due dates September 5, January 5 and April 5 [135](#cite:135) [137](#cite:137); NSF requires a Project Pitch first and funds Phase I up to $305,000 [35](#cite:35); DOE invites full applications only after a successful pitch [161](#cite:161); USDA, NIST and NOAA post their own notices [183](#cite:183) [208](#cite:208) [214](#cite:214).
Grant-agency notices are posted on [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov), which this guide harvests; SBIR.gov is linked but not harvested [12](#cite:12).

HHS limits a firm to nine Phase I, [Fast-Track](#term:fast-track) and [Direct to Phase II](#term:direct-to-phase-ii) applications per fiscal year; NSF 26-510 allows one proposal per organization [29](#cite:29) [35](#cite:35).

name: SBIR/STTR Phase I at a contract agency (DoD/DoW, NASA, DOT, EPA, ED, DHS)
governing_text: 15 U.S.C. 638; SBA SBIR/STTR Policy Directive (May 3, 2023); Pub. L. 119-83
what: The same program run as contracts: the agency publishes topics and the firm proposes against one, through the agency's portal, under a [solicitation](#term:solicitation) that is also [synopsized](#term:synopsis) on [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) [12](#cite:12) [52](#cite:52). The [Department of War](#term:department-of-war) accepts proposals only through [DSIP](#term:dsip) and ran six numbered releases in FY2026, though its page still describes three a year [52](#cite:52) [41](#cite:41). Amounts vary by component: [AFWERX](#term:afwerx) up to $323,000 for Phase I, DARPA typically $250K, the Army up to $300,000 on its page [64](#cite:64) [86](#cite:86) [81](#cite:81).
who_for: A firm whose technology matches a published topic; eligibility as for the [grant](#term:grant) agencies [10](#cite:10) [5](#cite:5).
how_it_works: Register in SAM, the [SBA company registry](#term:sbir-gov) and the agency portal (DSIP via login.gov for DoW; ProSAMS for [NASA](#term:agency-abbreviations)) [37](#cite:37) [36](#cite:36) [88](#cite:88) [168](#cite:168).

Read the release schedule: DoW Release 6 opened September 23, 2026 and closes October 21, 2026 [41](#cite:41); NASA runs appendices under [BAA](#term:baa) 80NSSC26R0003 [168](#cite:168); DOT, EPA and ED post annual solicitations [191](#cite:191) [201](#cite:201) [206](#cite:206).
Contact topic authors only during pre-release; once open, questions go through the portal's Q&A [52](#cite:52).
Contract-agency solicitations appear on SAM.gov, which this guide harvests; the DoW portal itself cannot be read by automated tools [52](#cite:52).

name: STTR with a research institution
governing_text: 15 U.S.C. 638; Policy Directive §6
what: [STTR](#term:sttr) funds the same phases as [SBIR](#term:sbir) but requires a formal partnership with a nonprofit research institution: the firm performs not less than 40 percent of the work and the institution not less than 30 percent, and the PI may be employed by either [5](#cite:5). Six agencies run STTR [12](#cite:12). The 2026 act extended [Direct to Phase II](#term:direct-to-phase-ii) to STTR [1](#cite:1).
who_for: A firm whose technology sits with a university or federal lab partner; the partner route record covers how such partnerships are formed [5](#cite:5).
how_it_works: Secure the research-institution agreement before proposing; the allocation of rights to intellectual property is part of it [5](#cite:5).

Apply under the agency's STTR [solicitation](#term:solicitation) ([NIH](#term:agency-abbreviations) PA-27-102; NSF 26-510; DoW releases carry both B and T topics) [137](#cite:137) [35](#cite:35) [61](#cite:61).

pending_changes.text: Directive revision due by April 13, 2027 [1](#cite:1) [7](#cite:7).

name: Direct to Phase II
governing_text: 15 U.S.C. 638(cc) as amended by Pub. L. 119-83; Policy Directive
what: An agency may make a [Phase II](#term:phase-ii) award to a firm that has established feasibility without a prior [Phase I](#term:phase-i) from that agency. The 2026 act runs the authority to September 30, 2031 and extends it to [DOE](#term:agency-abbreviations), NASA and [STTR](#term:sttr); the posted directive still shows the older list [1](#cite:1) [5](#cite:5).
who_for: A firm with feasibility already shown, by its own or other funded work, at NIH, DoW, ED, DOE or NASA [1](#cite:1) [5](#cite:5).
how_it_works: Each agency states its own [Direct to Phase II](#term:direct-to-phase-ii) terms in its [solicitation](#term:solicitation); NIH's are in its parent notice and ED issued a separate Direct to Phase II solicitation in 2026 [135](#cite:135) [206](#cite:206).
Ceiling without [SBA](#term:sba) approval is $2,153,927 as of April 2026 [11](#cite:11).

name: Phase III: sole-source follow-on from SBIR/STTR work
governing_text: 15 U.S.C. 638(r); Policy Directive §4(c)
what: Work that derives from, extends or completes earlier [SBIR](#term:sbir)/[STTR](#term:sttr) work, funded from other than SBIR/STTR money [5](#cite:5). Under 15 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 638(r)(4) an agency may award it [sole source](#term:sole-source) without a [FAR Part 6](#term:full-and-open-competition) justification, and the directive sets no limit on number, duration, type or dollar value and lifts the size limits [225](#cite:225) [230](#cite:230) [5](#cite:5). [GAO](#term:gao) found Phase III data unreliable, so its scale cannot be measured [242](#cite:242).
who_for: A firm with a completed [Phase I](#term:phase-i) or II whose results a buyer wants to field or extend; the buyer may be any agency or a prime [5](#cite:5).
how_it_works: The firm documents the derivation from its SBIR/STTR work; the award can be a contract, [subcontract](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) or other instrument [5](#cite:5) [225](#cite:225).
The 2026 act directs model contracts, contracting-officer training and [FPDS](#term:fpds) tracking, none yet found implemented [1](#cite:1).

name: Transition programs after Phase II (defense)
governing_text: Component program pages; 10 U.S.C. 4022 for OT-based follow-on
what: Defense components add matched money or procurement funds after a [Phase II](#term:phase-ii) so that a technology can be fielded: [AFWERX](#term:afwerx) [TACFI](#term:stratfi-tacfi) ($375,000–$2 million) and STRATFI ($3–15 million) with matching funds and a government submitter; Army CATALYST matching Army SBIR, customer and integrator funds 2:1:1; the Navy STP, an 11-month assistance program; ART, matching a DoW sponsor 1:1; and APFIT, $10–50 million of procurement funding that only a government organization can request [64](#cite:64) [66](#cite:66) [239](#cite:239) [235](#cite:235) [55](#cite:55) [108](#cite:108) [109](#cite:109).
who_for: A firm with an active or recent Phase II and a government sponsor willing to submit [66](#cite:66) [109](#cite:109).
how_it_works: Each program is sponsor-driven; the firm's role is to secure the sponsor and the match [66](#cite:66) [83](#cite:83).

name: Strategic Breakthrough award (Phase II tier added in 2026)
what: A new [Phase II](#term:phase-ii) tier of not more than $30,000,000 over not more than 48 months, requiring at least one prior Phase II and matching funds of not less than 100 percent; it sunsets September 30, 2031 [1](#cite:1). NIH runs it as PA-27-101 [140](#cite:140).
who_for: A prior Phase II awardee with matching funds [1](#cite:1).
how_it_works: Agencies with [SBIR](#term:sbir) spending over $100 million may fund it from up to 0.50 percent of extramural budget; the award is exempt from the award-size cap [1](#cite:1).

name: Total small-business set-aside (the Rule of Two)
governing_text: 15 U.S.C. 644(j)(1) (the band between the micro-purchase threshold and the simplified acquisition threshold); FAR 19.502-2(a) and (b); FAR 13.003(b); FAR 19.203; 13 CFR 125.2(f)
what: The contracting officer restricts a purchase to small businesses when offers are reasonably expected from two or more of them, the codified [Rule of Two](#term:rule-of-two) (FAR 19.502-2) [384](#cite:384). Between the micro-purchase threshold and the [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold) the purchase is set aside unless the contracting officer determines there is no reasonable expectation of two competitive small-business offers, and that band is also reserved by statute [384](#cite:384) [374](#cite:374). Above the simplified acquisition threshold the acquisition is set aside when offers are expected from at least two responsible small businesses and award will be at fair market prices [384](#cite:384).
who_for: Any firm that is small under the [NAICS](#term:naics) [size standard](#term:size-standard) on the [solicitation](#term:solicitation); no certification is needed for the general small-business set-aside.
how_it_works: Micro-purchase threshold (FAR 2.101): $15,000; $2,000 for construction; $2,500 for services; $25,000 (inside the United States) / $40,000 (outside) for the emergency categories [418](#cite:418)
Simplified acquisition threshold: $350,000, raised from $250,000 on October 1, 2025 by FAR Case 2024-001 [417](#cite:417) [340](#cite:340)

Above $15,000 and not over $350,000: set aside for small business unless the contracting officer determines there is not a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more small businesses (FAR 19.502-2(a); FAR 13.003(b); 15 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 644(j)(1)) [384](#cite:384) [438](#cite:438) [374](#cite:374)

Above $350,000: the contracting officer shall set the acquisition aside when there is a reasonable expectation of offers from at least two responsible small businesses and award at fair market prices (FAR 19.502-2(b)) [384](#cite:384)

Above the simplified acquisition threshold, the [8(a)](#term:eight-a), [HUBZone](#term:hubzone), [SDVOSB](#term:sdvosb) and [WOSB](#term:wosb) programs are considered before a general small-business set-aside, with no order of precedence among the four (FAR 19.203; 13 CFR 125.2(f)) [429](#cite:429) [431](#cite:431). At or below it, the small-business set-aside does not preclude 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB or WOSB awards (FAR 19.203(b)) [384](#cite:384)

The contracting officer coordinates with the [small business specialist](#term:osdbu) no later than 30 days before a solicitation (FAR 19.201) [428](#cite:428); [SBA](#term:sba)'s [procurement center representative](#term:pcr) recommends set-asides within 15 days of receiving an acquisition package and can appeal a rejected recommendation (FAR 19.402; 13 CFR 125.2(b)) [430](#cite:430) [431](#cite:431)

DoD, codified DFARS 219.502-2: construction (including maintenance and repairs) under $3.5 million, dredging under $2 million, and architect-engineer services for military construction or family housing under $1 million are set aside [448](#cite:448)
The [limitations on subcontracting](#term:limitations-on-subcontracting) apply to small-business set-asides above the simplified acquisition threshold [422](#cite:422)
Agencies advertise contracts over $25,000 on [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) [443](#cite:443)

name: Partial small-business set-aside
governing_text: FAR 19.502-3 (contracts other than multiple-award; not read in this sweep); FAR 19.502-4 (multiple-award contracts)

who_for: Small firms that can perform a severable portion of a larger requirement.
how_it_works: Discretionary; needs a divisible requirement and two expected small-business offers on the portion [419](#cite:419)

Under FAR 19.502-4: excludes construction and is not for [simplified acquisition procedures](#term:simplified-acquisition-procedures); the [solicitation](#term:solicitation) must identify the set-aside and non-set-aside portions [419](#cite:419)

name: Set-aside of an order under a multiple-award contract
governing_text: 15 U.S.C. 644(r)(2) (as cited in FAR 19.504; statute text not read); FAR 19.504; FAR 16.505(b)(2)(i)(F); 13 CFR 125.2(e)
what: Contracting officers may, at their discretion, set aside orders placed under multiple-award contracts for small businesses (FAR 19.504) [420](#cite:420). SBA's regulation likewise leaves the order set-aside to the contracting officer's discretion (13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 125.2(e)) [431](#cite:431).

how_it_works: Order set-asides are at the contracting officer's discretion, citing 15 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 644(r)(2) (FAR 19.504(a)) [420](#cite:420)
Above the simplified acquisition threshold ($350,000), the contracting officer first considers the socioeconomic programs (FAR 19.504(a)(3)) [420](#cite:420) [417](#cite:417)

Each contract holder gets a fair opportunity to be considered for each order exceeding the micro-purchase threshold ($15,000); orders may be set aside for small business under FAR 16.505(b)(2)(i)(F) [421](#cite:421) [418](#cite:418)

A firm small at contract award is small for each order, subject to the [rerepresentation](#term:recertification) rules [427](#cite:427); after a disqualifying recertification it is ineligible for later set-aside or reserved orders [291](#cite:291)

Protest of an order (FAR 16.505(a)(10)): only for an increase in scope, period or maximum value, or for orders over $10 million (civilian agencies) or $25 million (DoD, [NASA](#term:agency-abbreviations), Coast Guard), and only to [GAO](#term:gao) [421](#cite:421). GAO reports that section 885 of the [FY2025](#term:fiscal-year) [NDAA](#term:ndaa) raised the DoD threshold to $35 million [469](#cite:469)
The agency head designates a task-order and delivery-order ombudsman (FAR 16.505(b)(8)) [421](#cite:421)
DoD: a postaward debriefing is required for task orders and delivery orders valued at $15 million or more (DFARS 216.505) [449](#cite:449)

name: 8(a) sole source and 8(a) competition
what: An agency can award a contract to a certified 8(a) participant [without competition](#term:sole-source) below a dollar line, and competes the requirement among 8(a) firms above it ([FAR](#term:far) 19.805-1) [338](#cite:338). 13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 124.506 as displayed prints $7,000,000 (manufacturing NAICS) / $4,500,000 (all other) [331](#cite:331)
A requirement may not be split to stay under the threshold [338](#cite:338)

name: HUBZone sole source and price evaluation preference
what: A [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) can award to an SBA-certified HUBZone firm without competition below a dollar cap when offers would not be received from two or more HUBZone firms ([FAR](#term:far) 19.1306) [349](#cite:349). In [full and open competition](#term:full-and-open-competition), HUBZone offers get a price evaluation preference: a factor of 10 percent is added to other offers (FAR 19.1307) [433](#cite:433).
who_for: SBA-certified HUBZone firms (certifications.yaml: hubzone).
how_it_works: Sole source, codified FAR 19.1306: up to $8.5 million for manufacturing NAICS codes and $5.5 million for all other, options included, only when two HUBZone offers are not expected and the requirement is not currently in [8(a)](#term:eight-a) [349](#cite:349)
13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 126.612 as displayed prints $7,000,000 (manufacturing) / $4,500,000 (all other) [347](#cite:347)

Price evaluation preference, codified FAR 19.1307: a factor of 10 percent is added to all offers except those of HUBZone firms and other small businesses; not used where price is not a selection factor, where all fair and reasonable offers are accepted, or for the reserved portion of a multiple-award [solicitation](#term:solicitation); the HUBZone firm may waive it [433](#cite:433) [349](#cite:349)
13 CFR 126.613: the HUBZone price is deemed lower if it is not more than 10% above the large-business low offer; not applied where the low offeror is a small business [347](#cite:347)
HUBZone eligibility is tested on the date of the initial offer including price, not on the award date, except for sole source [346](#cite:346)

name: SDVOSB sole source (government-wide) and VA Veterans First
governing_text: FAR 19.1406; 13 CFR 128.404; in VA: sections 502 and 503 of Public Law 109-461, 38 U.S.C. 8127–8128, and VAAR subpart 819.70
what: A [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) in any agency can award to a certified service-disabled veteran-owned small business without competition below a dollar cap ([FAR](#term:far) 19.1406) [368](#cite:368). Inside the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Veterans First Contracting Program gives SDVOSBs and then VOSBs priority over the other small-business programs [369](#cite:369) [434](#cite:434).
who_for: SBA-certified SDVOSBs; in VA, certified VOSBs as well (certifications.yaml: vosb-sdvosb-vetcert).
how_it_works: Government-wide sole source, codified FAR 19.1406: up to $8.5 million for a requirement within the NAICS codes for manufacturing and $5 million for a requirement within any other [NAICS code](#term:naics), options included [368](#cite:368)
The firm must be designated in [SAM](#term:sam-gov) as SBA-certified, or have represented SDVOSB status in SAM and applied to [SBA](#term:sba) on or before December 31, 2023 [368](#cite:368)
SDVOSB [set-aside](#term:set-aside) (13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 128.404): a reasonable expectation of two responsible SDVOSB offers at fair market price [363](#cite:363)
VA priority (VAAR 819.7005): SDVOSB, then VOSB, then [8(a)](#term:eight-a)/[HUBZone](#term:hubzone), then other small-business set-asides [369](#cite:369)
VA set-aside (VAAR 819.7006/819.7007): when two or more certified SDVOSBs (or VOSBs) are expected at a fair and reasonable price [369](#cite:369)
VA sole source (VAAR 819.7008/819.7009): where the anticipated award price including options will not exceed $5 million [369](#cite:369)

VA: the firm must be certified and listed in the SBA certification database (VAAR 819.7003(b)(3)) [369](#cite:369), and the offeror must certify compliance with the [limitations on subcontracting](#term:limitations-on-subcontracting) (819.7004(b)) [434](#cite:434)
SDVOSB [status protests](#term:size-protest) go to SBA's [Office of Hearings and Appeals](#term:oha), whose decision is final (FAR 19.307) [463](#cite:463)

name: WOSB / EDWOSB set-aside and sole source
governing_text: FAR 19.1506; 13 CFR 127.503; 13 CFR 127.501 (eligible industries)
what: In industries [SBA](#term:sba) has designated by [NAICS code](#term:naics), a [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) can restrict competition to certified WOSBs or EDWOSBs, or award sole source below a dollar cap when two or more offers are not expected [355](#cite:355) [357](#cite:357).
who_for: SBA-certified WOSBs and EDWOSBs in the eligible NAICS codes (certifications.yaml: wosb-edwosb).
how_it_works: Sole source, codified [FAR](#term:far) 19.1506: up to $8.5 million for manufacturing NAICS codes and $5.5 million for a requirement within any other NAICS codes, options included, at a fair and reasonable price [357](#cite:357)
EDWOSB awards are for NAICS codes where WOSBs are underrepresented; WOSB awards for codes where they are substantially underrepresented [357](#cite:357) [354](#cite:354)

[Set-aside](#term:set-aside) (13 CFR 127.503): a reasonable expectation, based on [market research](#term:market-research), that two or more EDWOSBs (or WOSBs) will offer, and a fair and reasonable price [355](#cite:355)

pending_changes.text: FAR-overhaul numbering: the [RFO](#term:revolutionary-far-overhaul) [Part 13](#term:simplified-acquisition-procedures) [model deviation text](#term:class-deviation) issued September 18, 2025 is retitled "Simplified Procedures for Noncommercial Acquisitions", restates the small-business reservation at 13.102 and sends [micro-purchases](#term:micro-purchase-threshold) to subpart 12.4 (13.401) [396](#cite:396); RFO [Part 12](#term:far-part-12) (August 14, 2025, updated April 20, 2026) holds micro-purchase procedures at 12.4 [395](#cite:395). DoD adopted Parts 12 and 13 by Class Deviations 2026-O0028 and 2026-O0029, both dated 18 December 2025 [401](#cite:401).

[FAR](#term:far) Case 2026-003 would narrow Part 13 to noncommercial buys at or below the [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold) and transfer micro-purchase procedures from FAR subpart 13.2 to subpart 12.4; comments due October 19, 2026 [405](#cite:405).

conflicts: SBA's "Types of contracts" page says contracts under $150,000 are automatically set aside [385] vs the $350,000 simplified acquisition threshold [417](#cite:417)
name: Simplified acquisition and micro-purchase
what: Agencies use simplified acquisition procedures to the maximum extent practicable for purchases at or below the simplified acquisition threshold (FAR 13.003(a)) [438](#cite:438). Purchases between the micro-purchase threshold and the simplified acquisition threshold are [set aside](#term:set-aside) for small business (FAR 13.003(b)) [438](#cite:438). For micro-purchases the Governmentwide commercial purchase card is the preferred method, and almost no [clauses](#term:clause-numbering) apply (FAR 13.201) [440](#cite:440).
who_for: Any firm for micro-purchases; small businesses for purchases between the micro-purchase threshold and the simplified acquisition threshold.
how_it_works: Micro-purchase threshold (FAR 2.101): $15,000; $2,000 for construction; $2,500 for services; $25,000 (inside the United States) / $40,000 (outside) for the emergency categories [418]; raised from $10,000 on October 1, 2025 [417](#cite:417)
Simplified acquisition threshold: $350,000, raised from $250,000 on October 1, 2025 [417](#cite:417)

Above $15,000 and not over $350,000: reserved for small business unless two competitive small-business offers cannot be obtained (FAR 13.003(b); 15 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 644(j)(1)) [438](#cite:438) [374](#cite:374)

Micro-purchases: the purchase card is the preferred method to purchase and to pay (FAR 13.201(b)); no provisions or clauses are required except as at 13.202 and 32.1110 (FAR 13.201(d)) [440](#cite:440)

The card may be used by [contracting officers](#term:contracting-officer) and other designated individuals, for micro-purchases, for orders under existing contracts, and for payment (FAR 13.301) [441](#cite:441)
Purchase-card micro-purchases are among the listed exceptions to the [SAM registration](#term:sam-gov) requirement (FAR 4.1102) [302](#cite:302)

[GSA](#term:gsa) tells cardholders to check sources in order: personal property, UNICOR (mandatory over $3,500 unless waived), AbilityOne, then the commercial platforms, then open market [445](#cite:445); eight commercial platforms support purchases at or below the micro-purchase threshold [444](#cite:444)

Getting found: the SAM registration populates [SBA](#term:sba)'s Small Business Search; agencies advertise contracts over $25,000 on SAM.gov; [SubNet](#term:subnet) lists subcontracting opportunities posted by large [primes](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) [443](#cite:443)
Schedule contractors' catalogues are ordered through GSA Advantage, where federal buyers pay by purchase card or activity address code [446](#cite:446)

pending_changes.text: FAR-overhaul numbering: the [RFO](#term:revolutionary-far-overhaul) [Part 12](#term:far-part-12) [model deviation text](#term:class-deviation) (issued August 14, 2025, updated April 20, 2026) absorbs the simplified commercial procedures that sat in subpart 13.5: at 12.201-1(a), an [RFQ](#term:solicitation) followed by a purchase order for commercial acquisitions up to $9 million ($15 million for the emergency categories, 12.001(c)); 12.103 points to [Part 19](#term:far-part-19) for [set-asides](#term:set-aside) [395](#cite:395). DoD adopted it with [DFARS](#term:dfars) 212 by Class Deviation 2026-O0028, dated 18 December 2025 [401](#cite:401). RFO Part 7 (September 4, 2025) puts [commercial products](#term:commercial-product) and services first (7.102(b)(1)) and existing contracts before new awards (7.102(b)(4)) [394](#cite:394).

[FAR](#term:far) Case 2026-003 would restructure Part 12 into three process subparts with simplified commercial procedures up to $9 million ($15 million for specified emergencies), remove provisions 52.212-3 and 52.212-5, and add "required use" and "Best in Class" designations for existing vehicles in Part 8; comments due October 19, 2026 [405](#cite:405).

FAR Case 2026-002 would move [market research](#term:market-research) into subpart 7.2 and, at proposed 7.201(f), require agencies to procure commercial products and services to the maximum extent practicable "by following a specified order of available solutions"; comments closed July 23, 2026 [404](#cite:404).

name: Commercial product or commercial service buy
what: Agencies are to acquire commercial products, commercial services or nondevelopmental items when they are available to meet the agency's needs (FAR 12.101) [442](#cite:442). For commercial buys, [simplified procedures](#term:simplified-acquisition-procedures) may be used above the [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold) up to $9 million (FAR 13.500) [439](#cite:439).
who_for: Firms selling products or services that are also sold commercially.
how_it_works: FAR 12.101 puts three duties on the agency: market research; acquiring commercial or nondevelopmental items when available; and requiring [primes](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) and subcontractors to use them [442](#cite:442)

Codified FAR 13.500: simplified procedures in amounts greater than the simplified acquisition threshold ($350,000) but not exceeding $9 million, or $15 million for acquisitions described in 13.500(c) (contingency, cyber/CBRN defense, international disaster assistance, emergency or major disaster), including options [439](#cite:439) [438](#cite:438) [417](#cite:417)
The $9,000,000 ceiling rose from $7,500,000 on October 1, 2025 [417](#cite:417)

pending_changes.text: FAR-overhaul numbering: the [RFO](#term:revolutionary-far-overhaul) [Part 19](#term:far-part-19) [model deviation text](#term:class-deviation) issued September 26, 2025 carries the [subcontracting plan](#term:subcontracting-plan) at 19.109, required above $900,000 ($2 million for construction of any public facility), and names "[Subcontracting Plan Reporting](#term:isr-ssr) (SPR)" at [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) as the reporting system (19.001) [391](#cite:391). [GSA](#term:gsa) adopted it effective November 3, 2025 [400](#cite:400); DoD effective February 1, 2026 [402](#cite:402).

FAR-overhaul numbering: the RFO Part 19 model deviation text moves subcontracting plans to 19.109 (when required, at the same $900,000 / $2 million and with the same exemptions), 19.206 (evaluating plans) and 19.302 (postaward compliance; 19.302-2 keeps the willful or intentional definition); [clauses](#term:clause-numbering) 52.219-9, 52.219-16 and 52.219-14 are retained [391](#cite:391). GSA adopted it by Class Deviation RFO-2025-19, issued September 26, 2025 and effective November 3, 2025 [699](#cite:699). The codified [FAR](#term:far) ([FAC](#term:fac) 2026-01) is unchanged [692](#cite:692).

The model deviation text was amended on February 20, 2026 for the retirement of eSRS: reports go to Subcontracting Plan Reporting in SAM.gov and the ISR due date moves from 30 to 45 days [701](#cite:701) [699](#cite:699) [700](#cite:700). See the gate subcontracting-plan-reporting-sam.

Formal rulemaking: the [FAR Council](#term:far-council) said it "is issuing twelve [proposed rules](#term:proposed-rule) that collectively will streamline the FAR in its entirety" [403](#cite:403). Neither the first package (June 23, 2026) nor the second (September 18, 2026; comments due October 19, 2026) includes Part 19; the second covers Part 44 and Part 52 clauses [409](#cite:409), and the Parts 14, 28, 36 and 52 proposed rule (91 [FR](#term:federal-register) 59534) as fetched does not include 52.219-9 [703](#cite:703). Not checked after September 21, 2026.

[SBA](#term:sba) proposed (89 FR 103709, under section 862 of the FY2024 [NDAA](#term:ndaa)) to cut the past-due notice trigger from 90 to 30 days and to require [primes](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) to cooperate in correcting unjustified non-payment; comments closed February 18, 2025 [714](#cite:714). The Spring 2025 Unified Agenda showed it at [final rule](#term:final-rule) stage with an October 2025 target [715](#cite:715); 13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 125.3 as fetched on October 3, 2026 still says 90 days [704](#cite:704).

Lower-tier credit in the FAR: the FAR Council withdrew FAR Case 2018-003 on March 30, 2023 because the underlying statute had changed, and said a new FAR case would take the matter up [709](#cite:709); the 2019 proposal never became final [708](#cite:708) and the first SBA rule of 2016 was superseded [707](#cite:707). No replacement case was located.
Sunset: the DoD Comprehensive Subcontracting Plan Test Program expires on December 31, 2027 unless extended [717](#cite:717); GAO-16-27 reported 12 participants as of 2013 [752](#cite:752).

conflicts: Reporting system: eSRS in the codified clause 52.219-9 [437](#cite:437) vs "Subcontracting Plan Reporting (SPR)" at SAM.gov in the RFO text [391](#cite:391)

Plan threshold: $900,000 ($2 million for construction) in FAR 19.702 [692](#cite:692), in the 2025 inflation rule [340](#cite:340) and in USDA's 2026 directory [742](#cite:742) vs "in excess of $750,000, or in excess of $1,500,000 for construction of a public facility" in 13 CFR 125.3 [704](#cite:704) vs $950,000 ($2 million) in CRS R47585 as read on a mirror [749](#cite:749) vs $750,000 ($1.5 million) on DOT's directory page [740](#cite:740) and $850,000 ($1.5 million) on DOT's advice page [741](#cite:741)

Lower-tier credit: elective any-tier credit in 13 CFR 125.3(a)(1)(i)(C) [704](#cite:704) vs award data "limited to awards made to their immediate next-tier subcontractors" in codified FAR 52.219-9 [437](#cite:437)

Replaced-subcontractor duty: the FAR requires a written explanation within 30 days of contract completion [436](#cite:436); only the DoD clause requires notice when the substitution is made [718](#cite:718)
name: Subcontracting under a prime's small business subcontracting plan
what: A prime contractor that is not small must have a small business subcontracting plan on contracts above $900,000 ($2 million for construction) where subcontracting possibilities exist (FAR 19.702) [435](#cite:435). The plan sets goals, in dollars and percentages, for subcontracting to small, [veteran-owned](#term:sdvosb), service-disabled veteran-owned, [HUBZone](#term:hubzone), small disadvantaged and [women-owned small businesses](#term:wosb) (FAR 52.219-9) [437](#cite:437).
who_for: Small firms selling to large primes; the plan's goals are a reason primes look for them.
how_it_works: Plan required above $900,000 ($2 million for construction); not required from [small business concerns](#term:size-standard), for personal services, or for work wholly outside the United States [435](#cite:435)
The thresholds rose from $750,000 and $1,500,000 on October 1, 2025 [417](#cite:417)
A plan carries separate percentage goals by category and a statement of the total dollars planned to be subcontracted [436](#cite:436)
[Flowdown](#term:flow-down): subcontractors other than small with awards over $900,000 ($2 million for construction) adopt their own plan [436](#cite:436)
Reporting: ISR semi-annually and SSR annually by October 30, through eSRS [436](#cite:436) [437](#cite:437)
Failure to comply in good faith is a material breach and carries liquidated damages [435](#cite:435)

A firm may represent in good faith that it is a [small disadvantaged business](#term:sdb) for federal subcontracting programs [372](#cite:372); SDVOSBs may no longer [self-certify](#term:representations-and-certifications) for subcontracts that count toward SDVOSB subcontracting goals [367](#cite:367)
[SubNet](#term:subnet) lists subcontracting opportunities posted by large primes [443](#cite:443)

DoD ([DFARS](#term:dfars) 219.702-70): the Test Program for Comprehensive Subcontracting Plans needs three DoD contracts in the prior year totalling at least $100 million and expires December 31, 2027 [448](#cite:448)
Threshold: $900,000 ($2 million for construction), raised from $750,000 and $1.5 million by FAC 2025-06, effective October 1, 2025 [692](#cite:692) [340](#cite:340)

Three plan types (FAR 19.701): individual (one contract, whole period including options), commercial (the offeror's [fiscal year](#term:fiscal-year) and whole commercial production; "the preferred" approach for [commercial products](#term:commercial-product) and services) and master (all elements except goals; effective for three years after approval) [692](#cite:692) [436](#cite:436)

Clauses (FAR 19.708): 52.219-8 above the [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold); 52.219-9 above $900,000 ($2 million for construction); 52.219-16 wherever 52.219-9 is used; 52.219-10 as an optional incentive clause [692](#cite:692)
Flow-down: 52.219-8 goes into all subcontracts that offer further subcontracting opportunities, including commercial subcontracts under 52.244-6 [436](#cite:436) [695](#cite:695)

Good faith standard: failure means a "willful or intentional failure to perform ... or willful or intentional action to frustrate the plan"; missing a goal "does not, in and of itself, constitute a failure to make a good faith effort" (FAR 19.705-7) [692](#cite:692). A failure is a material breach, may be considered in any [past performance](#term:cpars) evaluation, and carries liquidated damages equal to the actual dollar amount by which the contractor failed to achieve each goal, after written notice and a chance to respond, with appeal under the Disputes clause [437](#cite:437) [694](#cite:694)
The examples of good faith and of failure came from SBA's rule 84 FR 65647 (effective December 30, 2019) and the FAR's FAC 2021-07 (effective September 10, 2021) [711](#cite:711) [712](#cite:712)
Indirect costs must be included in the goals if the contract exceeds $7.5 million (13 CFR 125.3(c)(1)(iv)) [704](#cite:704)

Lower-tier credit: under 13 CFR 125.3(a)(1)(i)(C) a prime may elect credit for small business subcontracts at any tier only where the goals pertain to a single contract with one Federal agency and the lower-tier subcontractors have their own individual plans (SBA final rule 88 FR 70339, effective November 13, 2023) [704](#cite:704) [710](#cite:710); the codified clause 52.219-9 limits reported award data to "immediate next-tier subcontractors", with lower-tier credit only through an [ANC](#term:entity-owned-firm) or Indian tribe designation [437](#cite:437)

DoD (DFARS 219.7): primes may count subcontracts to qualified nonprofit agencies for the blind and severely disabled, and mentor firms may count awards to [protégés](#term:mentor-protege-sba) toward small disadvantaged business goals; the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) must challenge any plan without positive goals, and an SDB goal below five percent needs approval one level above the contracting officer [716](#cite:716) [718](#cite:718)

DoD Test Program for comprehensive plans (DFARS 219.702-70): a contractor with at least three DoD contracts in the preceding fiscal year worth at least $100 million in aggregate may hold one corporate, division or plant-wide plan; clause 252.219-7004 is used in place of 52.219-9 and 52.219-16; "The Test Program expires on December 31, 2027." [717](#cite:717) [716](#cite:716) [719](#cite:719)

On a [set-aside](#term:set-aside) contract held by a small prime, work passed to a [similarly situated](#term:similarly-situated-entity) first-tier subcontractor does not count against the prime's [limitation on subcontracting](#term:limitations-on-subcontracting), but anything that subcontractor passes on does (FAR 52.219-14; 13 CFR 125.6) [423](#cite:423) [424](#cite:424)

Goals behind the plans: SBA negotiates each agency's small business subcontracting goal from recent achievement levels [747](#cite:747); subcontracting achievement is 20% of an agency's [scorecard](#term:goals) grade [383](#cite:383); GSA's FY 2026 subcontracting goal is 24% [748](#cite:748). [CRS](#term:crs), read on a mirror, reports that SBA sets the SDB, HUBZone, WOSB and SDVOSB goals at the statutory level and "bases subcontracting goals on recent achievement levels" [378](#cite:378)

Credit rests on the subcontractor's own representation: [GAO](#term:gao) found NNSA and its management and operating contractors counted about $1.1 billion of subcontracts as small business awards in fiscal years 2018-2022 when the recipients did not meet SBA size standards [754](#cite:754)

Oversight: SBA's [Commercial Market Representatives](#term:cmr) run compliance reviews and rate primes Exceptional, Very Good, Satisfactory, Marginal or Unsatisfactory (13 CFR 125.3(e)-(f)) [704](#cite:704). GAO found contracting officers did not ensure required subcontracting reports were filed on 14 of 26 contracts reviewed [750](#cite:750), that contracting officers "rarely identify contractors who have not met their small business goals" and that SBA conducted only six compliance reviews in each of fiscal years 2021 and 2022 [751](#cite:751)
benefits: The prime must make a good faith effort to buy from the small businesses it used in preparing the bid or proposal, "in the same or greater scope, amount, and quality", and give the contracting officer a written explanation within 30 days of contract completion if it does not (FAR 19.704(a)(12)-(13); 52.219-9(d)(12)-(d)(13)) [436](#cite:436) [437](#cite:437)
The prime may not prohibit a subcontractor from discussing payment or utilization matters with the contracting officer (FAR 19.704(a)(14); 52.219-9(d)(14)) [436](#cite:436) [437](#cite:437)

The prime must pay small business subcontractors on time and notify the contracting officer of a reduced or untimely payment (FAR 19.704(a)(15)) [436](#cite:436); under clause 52.242-5 untimely means more than 90 days past due and the written notice is due not later than 14 days after the event [698](#cite:698); 13 CFR 125.3(c)(5) carries the same 90 days [704](#cite:704)
Above the simplified acquisition threshold the prime must tell unsuccessful small business subcontract offerors who the apparent successful offeror is before award (52.219-9(e)(6)) [437](#cite:437)

A small first-tier subcontractor under a prime contract that included a subcontracting plan may ask the prime for a past performance rating within 30 calendar days after the prime contract's period of performance ends; the prime must provide it within 15 calendar days of the request, on a five-level scale, and the subcontractor may notify the contracting officer if the prime does not comply (13 CFR 125.11(c); 87 FR 43731) [713](#cite:713) [781](#cite:781)

DoD contracts: when a prime replaces a small firm identified in its plan with a firm that is not small, it must notify the Administrative Contracting Officer in writing (DFARS 219.704; 252.219-7003(e)) [716](#cite:716) [718](#cite:718)
requirements: The prime may accept a subcontractor's written representation of its size and socioeconomic status unless it has reason to question it; HUBZone status is confirmed in SAM or SBA's search database (52.219-8(e)) [693](#cite:693)

Plans are not required from small business concerns, for personal services contracts, or for contracts performed entirely outside the United States and its outlying areas (FAR 19.702(b)) [692](#cite:692); small primes cannot be required to submit a formal plan, but all primes must give small firms the maximum practicable opportunity (13 CFR 125.3(b)) [704](#cite:704)

A subcontractor that is not small and receives a subcontract in excess of $900,000 ($2 million for construction) must adopt its own 52.219-9 plan (FAR 19.704(a)(9)) [436](#cite:436); no plan is required from a subcontractor where the prime contract contains 52.212-5 or the subcontractor supplies a commercial product or service under 52.244-6 (52.219-9(j)) [437](#cite:437)
steps: Find primes that hold plans and their small business liaisons (see the route finding-subcontract-work) [732](#cite:732) [740](#cite:740)
Get into the prime's proposal: the good faith duty attaches to the small businesses the prime used in preparing the bid or proposal [436](#cite:436)
Give the prime a written representation of size and socioeconomic status; the prime may rely on it [693](#cite:693)
If the prime drops the firm or pays late, raise it with the contracting officer; the prime may not prohibit that [436](#cite:436)
Request a past performance rating from the prime within 30 calendar days after the prime contract's period of performance ends [781](#cite:781)

name: Size protest
what: An offeror, the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer), [SBA](#term:sba) or another [interested party](#term:bid-protest) may protest the small business [representation](#term:representations-and-certifications) of an offeror ([FAR](#term:far) 19.302) [458](#cite:458). Private parties have five business days after bid opening or notice of the apparent successful offeror [458](#cite:458) [294](#cite:294).
who_for: An offeror on a [set-aside](#term:set-aside) that believes the apparent winner is not small.
how_it_works: Who may file on a set-aside: any offeror not eliminated, the contracting officer, SBA area directors and other interested parties; on competitive [8(a)](#term:eight-a) awards: offerors, the contracting officer and the SBA District Director or designee (13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 121.1001) [293](#cite:293)

Filed with the contracting officer within 5 business days (excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays) after bid opening or notice of the apparent successful offeror [458](#cite:458) [294](#cite:294)
The contracting officer forwards it to the SBA Government Contracting Area Office for the challenged firm's headquarters; SBA decides within 15 business days [458](#cite:458)
Appeal to SBA's [Office of Hearings and Appeals](#term:oha) within 15 calendar days after receipt of the formal size determination; an untimely appeal is dismissed (13 CFR 134.304) [460](#cite:460)

Contracting officers and SBA are not bound by the time limit; premature and untimely protests are dismissed; after agency corrective action in a bid protest a new five-business-day window opens [294](#cite:294) [459](#cite:459)
8(a): size can be protested on competitive awards but not on [sole-source](#term:sole-source) ones [337](#cite:337)
[GAO](#term:gao) does not decide size, NAICS or [Certificate of Competency](#term:responsibility) matters; they belong to SBA (4 CFR 21.5(b)) [467](#cite:467)
Dollar thresholds and fees: none stated in the texts read

pending_changes.text: FAR-overhaul numbering: the [status protest](#term:size-protest) sections and their deadlines were not confirmed in the [RFO](#term:revolutionary-far-overhaul) [Part 19](#term:far-part-19) [model deviation text](#term:class-deviation) (issued September 26, 2025) as read [391](#cite:391).

name: Status protest (HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB/EDWOSB)
what: An [interested party](#term:bid-protest) may challenge the [HUBZone](#term:hubzone), [SDVOSB](#term:sdvosb) or [WOSB](#term:wosb)/EDWOSB status of the apparent successful offeror on a program award [462](#cite:462) [463](#cite:463) [464](#cite:464). The deadline in each case is the fifth business day after bid opening or the notice of the apparent successful offeror [462](#cite:462) [463](#cite:463) [464](#cite:464). [8(a)](#term:eight-a) eligibility cannot be challenged by another participant or any other party [337](#cite:337).
who_for: An offeror on a HUBZone, SDVOSB or WOSB/EDWOSB award that believes the apparent winner does not hold the status.
how_it_works: HUBZone ([FAR](#term:far) 19.306): by the fifth business day; forwarded to [SBA](#term:sba)'s HUBZone Program Director (hzprotests@sba.gov); decision in 15 business days; appeal to the AA/GC&BD within 5 business days; on a [sole source](#term:sole-source) only SBA or the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) may protest [462](#cite:462). SBA and contracting officer protests are always timely, and specific facts are required [348](#cite:348)

SDVOSB (FAR 19.307): by the fifth business day; [VA](#term:agency-abbreviations) or SBA may protest at any time; forwarded to SBA's [Office of Hearings and Appeals](#term:oha) (OHAfilings@sba.gov), whose decision is effective immediately and final [463](#cite:463) [365](#cite:365)

WOSB/EDWOSB (FAR 19.308): by the fifth business day; forwarded to SBA (wosbprotest@sba.gov); SBA decides within 15 business days; appeal to OHA within 10 business days [464](#cite:464). A protest without specific facts or allegations is insufficient [356](#cite:356), and only certified WOSBs or pending applicants may protest [360](#cite:360)
OHA decides size and [NAICS](#term:naics) appeals, VOSB/SDVOSB status protests and appeals, WOSB/EDWOSB appeals, and 8(a) eligibility, suspension and termination appeals [461](#cite:461)
Dollar thresholds and fees: none stated in the texts read

pending_changes.text: [FAR](#term:far) Case 2026-001 (91 [FR](#term:federal-register) 37550) rewrites Part 33: [contracting officers](#term:contracting-officer) report agency [protests](#term:bid-protest) to the head of the contracting activity; protesters may ask for independent review above the contracting officer; redacted technical evaluation and source-selection documents may be disclosed; comments closed July 23, 2026 [403](#cite:403). The [RFO](#term:revolutionary-far-overhaul) [model deviation text](#term:class-deviation) for Part 33 was not read in this sweep, so no deviation numbering is recorded.

name: Agency-level protest
what: An interested party can protest to the agency itself, filing with the contracting officer and, on request, getting an independent review at a level above the contracting officer (FAR 33.103) [465](#cite:465). Pursuing an agency protest does not extend the time for obtaining a stay at [GAO](#term:gao) [465](#cite:465).
who_for: An offeror or prospective offeror objecting to a [solicitation](#term:solicitation)'s terms or to an award.
how_it_works: Timing: protests of solicitation defects before bid opening or the closing date; other grounds within 10 days of when the basis is known [465](#cite:465)
The agency aims to resolve the protest within 35 days [465](#cite:465)
A protest within 10 days of award suspends performance [465](#cite:465)
A later GAO protest must be filed within 10 days after adverse agency action on the agency protest (4 [CFR](#term:cfr) 21.2) [467](#cite:467)
Fees: the sweep describes the agency-level protest as free [465](#cite:465); no dollar threshold applies in the text read

pending_changes.text: In its response to section 885 of the [FY2025](#term:fiscal-year) [NDAA](#term:ndaa), [GAO](#term:gao) proposed a clearer pleading standard ("protesters must provide, at a minimum, credible allegations that are supported by evidence") and did not endorse fee shifting [469](#cite:469). The extract of 4 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 21 as of September 28, 2026 showed no 2025–26 amendment [467](#cite:467).

[FAR](#term:far) Case 2026-001 would replace the GAO procedure text in FAR Part 33 with a pointer to 4 CFR part 21; comments closed July 23, 2026 [403](#cite:403). The [RFO](#term:revolutionary-far-overhaul) [model deviation text](#term:class-deviation) for Part 33 was not read in this sweep, so no deviation numbering is recorded.

Pointer only, not verified in a primary source: a law-firm newsletter reports that section 875 of the FY2026 NDAA lets DoD withhold up to 5% of payments from an incumbent that [protests](#term:bid-protest) at GAO and keeps performing, awaiting [DFARS](#term:dfars) rulemaking [471](#cite:471).

conflicts: DoD task- and delivery-order protest threshold: $25 million in codified FAR 16.505(a)(10) [421] vs $35 million per GAO's account of section 885 of the FY2025 NDAA [469](#cite:469); neither the DFARS nor the RFO text carrying $35 million was found [449](#cite:449) [397](#cite:397)
name: GAO bid protest
what: An actual or prospective bidder or offeror whose direct economic interest would be affected by the award of a contract can protest to the Government Accountability Office under 4 CFR part 21 [467](#cite:467). GAO decides within 100 days of filing, or 65 days under the express option [466](#cite:466).
who_for: An offeror or prospective offeror with a direct economic interest in the award.
how_it_works: Filed through GAO's Electronic Protest Docketing System (4 CFR 21.1) [467](#cite:467); the filing fee is $500 effective October 1, 2024 ($350 before) [468](#cite:468)

Timing (4 CFR 21.2): [solicitation](#term:solicitation) defects before bid opening or the proposal due date; otherwise 10 days after the basis is known; 10 days after a required [debriefing](#term:debriefing); 10 days after adverse agency action on an agency protest [467](#cite:467)
Stay of award or performance when the agency is notified within 10 days after award or 5 days after a debriefing date [466](#cite:466)
The agency report is due within 30 days [466](#cite:466)
The attorney fee cap of $150 per hour applies to firms other than small businesses [466](#cite:466)

Outside GAO's review: size, [NAICS](#term:naics) and [Certificate of Competency](#term:responsibility) matters belong to [SBA](#term:sba) (4 CFR 21.5(b)); orders are outside GAO's jurisdiction except as statute allows (21.5(l)) [467](#cite:467)

Orders under task- and delivery-order contracts can be protested only for an increase in scope, period or maximum value, or above $10 million (civilian agencies) and, in the codified FAR, $25 million (DoD, [NASA](#term:agency-abbreviations), Coast Guard) (FAR 16.505(a)(10)) [421](#cite:421); GAO reports that section 885 of the FY2025 NDAA raised the DoD figure to $35 million [469](#cite:469)
FY2025 figures: 1,688 cases filed, a 14% sustain rate and a 52% effectiveness rate [470](#cite:470)

name: Finding subcontract work (SubNet, prime directories, LYNX, Commercial Market Representatives)
governing_text: No regulation governs the directories (SBA, GSA and agency services). 13 CFR 125.3(e) for Commercial Market Representatives; FAR subpart 4.14 and clause 52.204-10 for the public first-tier subcontract records.
what: SubNet is SBA's "database of subcontracting opportunities posted by large contractors looking for small businesses to serve as [subcontractors](#term:prime-and-subcontractor)" [443](#cite:443). SBA also publishes a directory of prime contractors that hold contracts with [subcontracting plans](#term:subcontracting-plan), and agency small business offices publish their own prime directories [732](#cite:732) [730](#cite:730). SBA's [Commercial Market Representatives](#term:cmr) "ensure small businesses get their fair share of opportunities as subcontractors" [733](#cite:733).
who_for: Small firms building a target list of primes by [NAICS code](#term:naics), agency or place, or looking for posted subcontract [solicitations](#term:solicitation).
how_it_works: SubNet, status on October 3, 2026: live with current listings (10 per page, at least 9 pages; first-page closing dates October 12 to November 17, 2026) on legacy.sba.gov, to which https://www.sba.gov/subnet and the old subnet.sba.gov address redirect; no retirement or replacement notice was found [731](#cite:731). It lets large businesses with federal contracts and subcontracting plans "post current subcontracting opportunities for small businesses" [736](#cite:736); large firms that want to post are told to email subcontracting@sba.gov [730](#cite:730) [731](#cite:731)

SBA Directory of Federal Government Prime Contractors with Subcontracting Plans: a spreadsheet on legacy.sba.gov; the newest file is [FY](#term:fiscal-year) 2024 (page updated March 4, 2025), FY 2018 to FY 2023 are also posted, information is removed after five years, and no FY 2025 file was posted as of October 3, 2026 [732](#cite:732)

[GSA](#term:gsa) Subcontracting Directory: it "Lists other than small business prime contractors who have been awarded contracts with us" [737](#cite:737); the file is downloadable from data.gov, declared quarterly, with the newest file named "SubK Directory as of 03132025 Filtered.xlsx" [739](#cite:739); the small firm then contacts the prime directly [738](#cite:738)
LYNX: SBA's page links https://www.lynxconnect.io/ and describes it as a "[Department of War](#term:department-of-war)" market-research platform [730](#cite:730); the LYNX site itself was not fetched

Agency directories: [DOT](#term:agency-abbreviations)'s FY 2026 directory of primes with approved plans [740](#cite:740) and its Procurement Assistance Division at (202) 366-1930 or (800) 532-1169 [741](#cite:741); USDA's 2026 directory of roughly 22 primes [742](#cite:742); NASA's prime-contractor pages (BAE Systems, Blue Origin, JPL, KBR on the fetch date) [743](#cite:743); DOE, where approximately 80% of the annual procurement base goes to management and operating contracts and a Small Business Program Manager directory lists DOE and M&O contacts [744](#cite:744); VA's Prime Contractor Directory, of which the one referenced is fiscal year 2020 [745](#cite:745)

Commercial Market Representatives match contractors with small firms, counsel, and run Subcontracting Orientation and Assistance Reviews and compliance reviews (13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 125.3(e)) [704](#cite:704) [735](#cite:735). The public contact route is subcontracting@sba.gov; the page gives no individual names or phone numbers [733](#cite:733). The only by-area CMR list found is a Word file from April 2020 [734](#cite:734); the current [Procurement Center Representative](#term:pcr) directory shows SBA's six government-contracting areas (Area 3 Southeast includes Alabama) [432](#cite:432)

Other tools SBA and DoD offices name: SBA's Small Business Search (formerly Dynamic Small Business Search) at https://search.[certifications.sba.gov](#term:mysba-certifications)/ and [APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs)](#term:apex-accelerator) [443](#cite:443) [733](#cite:733) [746](#cite:746)

Who subcontracts to whom: [USAspending](#term:usaspending) shows subawards through the subaward toggle in Advanced Search, award profile pages and the Custom Award Data download [728](#cite:728); [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) has a public subcontract API [725](#cite:725) [727](#cite:727). USAspending warns that "Duplication of subaward records is common" and that records are sometimes late, incomplete or inconsistent [728](#cite:728); data submitted one day is available to USAspending the next day and published the day after [729](#cite:729)

Where subcontract dollars go by industry: GSA's fiscal year 2025 report under [Small Business Act](#term:small-business-act) section 15(h)(3)(A)(ii) lists subcontract dollars by NAICS code for 300+ codes [755](#cite:755)
benefits: SubNet lists description, closing date, performance start date, place of performance, NAICS code and point of contact, filtered by state or keyword [731](#cite:731)
SBA's prime directory gives vendor name, location, contracting agency, product/service code, NAICS, contract number, performance dates and total contract value [732](#cite:732)

Agency directories name each prime's small business liaison: DOT's lists company, address, liaison name and phone and the work available for subcontracting [740](#cite:740); USDA's gives liaison contact, major products and services, subcontracting opportunities, contract number and dollar amount [742](#cite:742)
Published first-tier subcontract records show the prime contract number, subcontractor name and [UEI](#term:uei), amount, date, description and place of performance [727](#cite:727)
requirements: SubNet: questions go to the posted point of contact for the opportunity, not SBA [731](#cite:731)
SAM.gov subcontract reports: non-federal users sign in to search [726](#cite:726); the public API needs an API key, and non-federal users without an entity role get 10 requests a day [727](#cite:727)

Download SBA's FY 2024 prime directory and filter by NAICS code and contracting agency [732](#cite:732)
Download the GSA Subcontracting Directory file from data.gov and contact the prime directly [739](#cite:739) [738](#cite:738)
For one agency's supply chain, open that agency's directory and call the listed small business liaison [740](#cite:740) [742](#cite:742)
Look up a prime's existing first-tier subcontracts in USAspending or through the SAM.gov public subcontract API [728](#cite:728) [727](#cite:727)
Email subcontracting@sba.gov for subcontracting assistance from a Commercial Market Representative [733](#cite:733)

pending_changes.text: The second set of FAR-overhaul [proposed rules](#term:proposed-rule) (September 18, 2026; comments due October 19, 2026) covers Part 9 together with Parts 27 and 47 [409](#cite:409). Neither the proposed Part 9 text nor the [RFO](#term:revolutionary-far-overhaul) [model deviation text](#term:class-deviation) for Part 9 was read in these sweeps, so no class-deviation numbering is recorded for [FAR](#term:far) 9.601 to 9.604; the codified text cited is [FAC](#term:fac) 2026-01 [761](#cite:761).

The FTC and DOJ opened a joint inquiry toward replacement guidance on business collaborations (docket ATR-2026-0001); comments were due April 24, 2026, the listed topics do not name government-contract [teaming](#term:teaming-agreement), and no new guidance was found [829](#cite:829).

conflicts: GSA states "FAR subpart 9.6, Contractor Team Arrangements, does not apply to MAS CTA agreements" [762](#cite:762), although FAR subpart 9.6 uses the same term [761](#cite:761)
name: Teaming and contractor team arrangements (FAR 9.6, Small Business Teaming Arrangements, GSA MAS CTAs)
governing_text: FAR 9.601 to 9.604; provision FAR 52.207-6 (Aug 2024) and 13 CFR 121.103(b)(9) for Small Business Teaming Arrangements; provision FAR 52.203-2; GSA Multiple Award Schedule program guidance for Schedule CTAs (GSA states FAR subpart 9.6 does not apply to them)
what: FAR 9.601 recognises two forms of [contractor team arrangement](#term:cta): two or more companies form a partnership or [joint venture](#term:joint-venture) to act as a potential [prime contractor](#term:prime-and-subcontractor), or a potential prime agrees with other companies to have them act as its subcontractors under a specified contract [761](#cite:761). The Government recognises such arrangements provided they are identified and the company relationships are fully disclosed in the offer (FAR 9.603) [761](#cite:761). A [GSA Schedule](#term:mas) Contractor Team Arrangement is a different thing: two or more Multiple Award Schedule contractors team on a single requirement and each operates as a prime contractor for the portion of work it performs [762](#cite:762).
who_for: Any offeror that needs complementary capability (FAR 9.6); small firms bidding together on bundled or large [multiple-award contracts](#term:idiq) (Small Business Teaming Arrangement); Multiple Award Schedule contract holders (Schedule CTA).
how_it_works: Timing: arrangements are normally formed before the offer but may be entered later, including after award (FAR 9.602) [761](#cite:761)

Schedule CTA: the government is not involved in drafting the CTA document; [GSA](#term:gsa) "strongly encourages" submitting it in response to an [RFQ](#term:solicitation) [763](#cite:763); for [FPDS](#term:fpds) reporting the ordering agency determines which party receives the preponderance of revenue [762](#cite:762)

Antitrust enforcement: DOJ's Procurement Collusion Strike Force, established November 2019, pursues bid rigging, price fixing and market allocation in government procurement and reports 200+ investigations opened and 85+ guilty pleas and trial convictions as of April 30, 2026; its page does not mention teaming agreements or joint ventures [827](#cite:827)

Guidance gap: on December 11, 2024 the FTC and DOJ withdrew the April 2000 Antitrust Guidelines for Collaborations Among Competitors, saying they "no longer provide reliable guidance about how enforcers assess the legality of collaborations involving competitors." [828](#cite:828)

Where a teaming-style deal becomes bid rigging, in DOJ's words: a July 9, 2025 Sherman Act indictment alleged a would-be competitor agreed to "stand down and neither submit nor join an independent competing bid" in exchange for subcontracts; it concerned a state-university procurement, not a federal one, and the page notes a later presidential pardon [830](#cite:830) (press release located through a law-firm note [831](#cite:831))
benefits: "The Government will not normally require or encourage the dissolution of contractor team arrangements." (FAR 9.603) [761](#cite:761)

Small Business Teaming Arrangement: on bundled or multiple-award contracts above the substantial bundling threshold, a small prime may team with small subcontractors without [affiliation](#term:affiliation) if each member is small (13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 121.103(b)(9)) [770](#cite:770)
A prime may use a subcontractor's experience and [past performance](#term:cpars), including an incumbent's, to strengthen its offer (13 CFR 121.103(h)(3)(ii)) [706](#cite:706)

Schedule CTA: each team member has privity of contract with the government and can interact with it directly [763](#cite:763); each member reports its own sales and pays its own [Industrial Funding Fee](#term:iff) [762](#cite:762)
requirements: FAR 9.603: identify the arrangement and fully disclose the company relationships in the offer, or before the arrangement becomes effective if it is formed after the offer [761](#cite:761)

FAR 9.604: the Government may still require consent to subcontracts, determine the prime's responsibility, pursue competitive contracting, subcontracting and component breakout, and hold the prime fully responsible; "Nothing in this subpart authorizes contractor team arrangements in violation of antitrust statutes" [761](#cite:761)

Every offeror certifies under FAR 52.203-2 that its prices were arrived at independently, were not knowingly disclosed to another offeror or competitor, and that it made no attempt to induce another concern to submit or not submit an offer for the purpose of restricting competition; the provision text does not specifically address joint or team proposals (per the extract) [765](#cite:765)

Small Business Teaming Arrangement (FAR 52.207-6): two or more small businesses in a joint venture, or a small prime with small subcontractors under a written agreement designated as a Small Business Teaming Arrangement that sets out responsibilities, roles and percentages of work [764](#cite:764)

Schedule CTA: every team member is a MAS contractor with its own MAS contract number [762](#cite:762); for a small-business set-aside order the lead and all members must meet the specified socioeconomic status [762](#cite:762), and "All members of the CTA must be small for the CTA to be eligible for that order." [763](#cite:763)

Schedule CTA agreement elements GSA lists: parties and MAS contract numbers; lead and members; team responsibilities; duration and options; ordering procedures; invoicing and payment; independent-contractor relationship; confidential information; conflict resolution favouring MAS terms; member replacement; each member reporting its own sales and paying its own IFF; pricing at or below MAS rates; signatures [762](#cite:762)

Prime-subcontractor teaming on a set-aside is tested under the ostensible subcontractor rule and the limitations on subcontracting (see the gate ostensible-subcontractor-affiliation) [770](#cite:770) [424](#cite:424)
steps: Prime-subcontractor team or joint venture under FAR 9.6: agree the roles, then identify the arrangement and disclose the relationships in the offer [761](#cite:761)
Small Business Teaming Arrangement: put it in a written agreement so designated, with responsibilities, roles and percentages of work [764](#cite:764)
Schedule CTA: draft the CTA document covering the elements GSA lists and submit it with the quote [762](#cite:762) [763](#cite:763)

pending_changes.text: FAR-overhaul numbering: in the [RFO](#term:revolutionary-far-overhaul) [Part 19](#term:far-part-19) [model deviation text](#term:class-deviation) the [joint venture](#term:joint-venture) provisions sit under the program sections, 19.105-1(c) ([HUBZone](#term:hubzone)), 19.106-1(c) ([SDVOSB](#term:sdvosb)) and 19.107-1(c) ([WOSB](#term:wosb)), and [rerepresentation](#term:recertification) is at 19.301; the codified location is [FAR](#term:far) 19.301-1(a)(2) [391](#cite:391) [766](#cite:766). Slice B captured no date on the page; September 26, 2025 is the issue date of [GSA](#term:gsa)'s Class Deviation RFO-2025-19 adopting the model text (effective November 3, 2025) [699](#cite:699). Other agencies' deviation memos were not read.

FAR Case 2023-015, Policy on Joint Ventures (RIN 9000-AO64), would implement [SBA](#term:sba)'s April 27, 2023 rule: change joint venture recertification procedures, bar one partner from being in more than one joint venture bidding on the same [solicitation](#term:solicitation), and adjust the award-eligibility period. It was at proposed-rule stage in the Fall 2024 Unified Agenda with an [NPRM](#term:proposed-rule) target of July 2025; no NPRM was located and the RIN was listed through the Spring 2025 agenda only [769](#cite:769).

Correction 90 [FR](#term:federal-register) 23609, effective June 4, 2025, changed the cross-reference in 13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 125.8 from 121.103(h)(4) to 121.103(b); it is the only 2025 Federal Register document found that touches 125.8 or 125.12 [784](#cite:784).

[Final rule](#term:final-rule) 89 FR 102448 (RIN 3245-AH68), effective January 16, 2025, created the consolidated recertification rule at 13 CFR 125.12 and made an [ostensible subcontractor](#term:ostensible-subcontractor) relationship a ground of ineligibility rather than treatment as a joint venture; the parts of the document amending 125.8 and 125.9 were beyond the extract [292](#cite:292).

conflicts: Financial statements to SBA: annual, "not later than 45 days after each operating year", in 13 CFR 125.8 [773](#cite:773) and on SBA's joint ventures page [789](#cite:789) vs quarterly, not later than 45 days after each operating quarter, in 13 CFR 124.513, 126.616, 127.506 and 128.402 [774](#cite:774) [776](#cite:776) [778](#cite:778) [779](#cite:779)
name: Joint venture for a small-business or socioeconomic set-aside
what: A joint venture is an association formed to carry out business ventures for joint profit over a two-year period; it must be in writing, do business under its own name and be identified as a joint venture in [SAM](#term:sam-gov) (13 CFR 121.103(h)) [770](#cite:770). It may submit an offer as small if each partner is small under the contract's [NAICS](#term:naics) [size standard](#term:size-standard), and a joint venture between a [protégé](#term:mentor-protege-sba) and its SBA-approved mentor is small if the protégé is small and the agreement meets the applicable section (13 CFR 121.103(h)(2); FAR 19.301-1(a)(2)) [770](#cite:770) [766](#cite:766). A joint venture agreement between firms that each qualify as small "need not be in any specific form or contain any specific conditions" (13 CFR 125.8(b)(1)) [773](#cite:773).
who_for: Two or more firms that are each small under the contract's NAICS code; a protégé with an SBA-approved mentor; a certified [8(a)](#term:eight-a), HUBZone, WOSB/EDWOSB or VOSB/SDVOSB firm leading a joint venture for that program's contracts.
how_it_works: Timing of the tests: size is determined as of the initial offer that includes price; compliance with the joint venture agreement requirements is judged as of the final proposal revision (negotiated) or final bid (sealed bidding) (13 CFR 121.404(a), (f)) [771](#cite:771)

The contract is executed in the joint venture's name (separate legal entity) or the small business's name (informal joint venture) and identified as a small-business joint venture award (13 CFR 125.8(f)) [773](#cite:773)

Before performance, a written certification signed by an authorised official of each partner goes to the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) and SBA (13 CFR 125.8(d)); an annual performance-of-work report and a completion report go to the contracting officer and SBA (13 CFR 125.8(h)) [773](#cite:773)

Recertification: a joint venture may recertify as small where all parties are small at recertification, or the protégé is small in a mentor-protégé joint venture (13 CFR 125.12(f)) [291](#cite:291); once the protégé is no longer small for the contract's NAICS code the joint venture cannot recertify as small, though a change in the protégé's size does not generally affect contracts already awarded (13 CFR 125.9(d)(1)) [785](#cite:785); [clause](#term:clause-numbering) FAR 52.219-28 carries separate joint venture [representations](#term:representations-and-certifications) for WOSB/EDWOSB, SDVOSB and HUBZone joint ventures [767](#cite:767)

[Protests](#term:bid-protest): a [size protest](#term:size-protest) against a joint venture awardee may come from any offeror not eliminated for reasons unrelated to size, the contracting officer or SBA [772](#cite:772) [766](#cite:766); a HUBZone joint venture protest is due by close of business on the fifth business day after notification of the apparent successful offeror [777](#cite:777); a VOSB/SDVOSB joint venture can be protested at [OHA](#term:oha) for failing 13 CFR 128.402, and losing on that ground alone does not affect the partner's own eligibility [780](#cite:780)

Sanctions: failing to have a compliant agreement, to perform to it or to the 40% rule, or to submit certifications or allow inspection are grounds for suspension or [debarment](#term:responsibility) (13 CFR 125.8(i)) [773](#cite:773); exceeding the [limitations on subcontracting](#term:limitations-on-subcontracting) carries a penalty of the greater of $500,000 or the excess spent on [subcontractors](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) (13 CFR 125.6(h)) [424](#cite:424)
The FAR took in SBA's joint venture rules by [FAC](#term:fac) 2022-08 (87 FR 58219), effective October 28, 2022 [768](#cite:768)
benefits: A joint venture may qualify for award under FAR subparts 19.8, 19.13, 19.14 and 19.15 [766](#cite:766)

Agencies must consider the work and qualifications of each partner and of the joint venture itself, and may not require the protégé to meet individually the same evaluation or responsibility criteria as other offerors (13 CFR 125.8(e)) [773](#cite:773)

A small business without its own [past performance](#term:cpars) may use that of a joint venture it belonged to, naming the joint venture contracts and the duties it carried out; it cannot claim work performed exclusively by other partners (13 CFR 125.11(b)) [781](#cite:781)

Within two years of its first award a joint venture may receive any number of contracts (the three-contracts-in-two-years limit was removed in 2020), and orders under a previously awarded contract may be issued beyond the two-year period [782](#cite:782) [770](#cite:770) [783](#cite:783)
A joint venture may be awarded a contract requiring a [facility clearance](#term:facility-clearance) where the joint venture itself or the lead small-business partner holds it [782](#cite:782)
requirements: Written agreement, own name, identified as a joint venture in SAM; it may be a formal or informal partnership or a separate legal entity (13 CFR 121.103(h)(1)) [770](#cite:770). SBA's page adds that the joint venture is registered in SAM.gov with its own UEI and CAGE code and the partners listed as immediate owners [789](#cite:789)

Unpopulated: a separate-legal-entity joint venture cannot be populated with individuals intended to perform set-aside contracts unless all parties are similarly situated; it may have its own employees for administrative functions, including Facility Security Officers [770](#cite:770)

Two-year rule: a specific joint venture generally may not be awarded contracts beyond two years from the award of its first contract, after which the partners are deemed affiliated for new offers; an offer submitted before the two years end may still be awarded, and the same partners may form a new joint venture with its own two-year period [770](#cite:770)
Size arithmetic: each partner counts its proportionate share of the joint venture's receipts and employees (13 CFR 121.103(h)(4)) [770](#cite:770)

Mentor-protégé joint venture: SBA must approve the mentor-protégé agreement before the joint venture submits an offer [785](#cite:785) [789](#cite:789); the agreement must contain the twelve provisions of 13 CFR 125.8(b)(2) (see the gate jv-agreement-requirements) [773](#cite:773)

Work share: the joint venture must meet the limitations on subcontracting in 13 CFR 125.6, performed by the joint venture participants in aggregate, and the protégé must perform at least 40% of the work the joint venture performs, more than administrative or ministerial functions [773](#cite:773) [423](#cite:423)

Program joint ventures: the certified firm is managing venturer, owns at least 51% and performs at least 40% [774](#cite:774) [776](#cite:776) [778](#cite:778) [779](#cite:779); "SBA does not certify HUBZone joint ventures" or VOSB/SDVOSB joint ventures [776](#cite:776) [779](#cite:779); SBA must approve an 8(a) joint venture before a sole-source 8(a) award and will not approve joint ventures for competitive 8(a) awards [774](#cite:774); an 8(a) protégé's joint venture with its mentor on 8(a) contracts must meet 13 CFR 124.513(c) and (d) [775](#cite:775)

A HUBZone, WOSB/EDWOSB or VOSB/SDVOSB firm cannot be a partner in more than one joint venture bidding on the same contract [776](#cite:776) [778](#cite:778) [779](#cite:779); a mentor with more than one protégé cannot submit competing offers on the same procurement through separate joint ventures, or hold the same small-business multiple-award contract through joint ventures with two protégés (13 CFR 125.9(b)(3)(i), (b)(4)) [785](#cite:785)
steps: Write the agreement: no prescribed form where every partner is small; the twelve listed provisions for a mentor-protégé joint venture [773](#cite:773)
Register the joint venture in SAM.gov under its own name with its own [UEI](#term:uei) and [CAGE code](#term:cage-code), designated as a joint venture [789](#cite:789) [770](#cite:770)
For a mentor-protégé joint venture, have the mentor-protégé agreement approved by SBA before the joint venture submits an offer [785](#cite:785)
Represent size at the initial offer that includes price [771](#cite:771)
Send the pre-performance certification to the contracting officer and SBA, then the annual and completion performance-of-work reports [773](#cite:773)
Questions go to the local SBA District Office [789](#cite:789)

The part of that rule amending 125.9 was beyond the extract [292](#cite:292).

The primary notice was not located and the outcome in the December 2024 final rule could not be read [292](#cite:292).

conflicts: Mentors at one time: SBA's page says a protégé may have two mentors at the same time (and no more than two over the life of the business) [788](#cite:788); 13 CFR 125.9(c)(2) says generally one at a time, a second only with SBA approval [785](#cite:785)
