name: SBA Mentor-Protégé Program
governing_text: 15 U.S.C. 657r; 13 CFR 125.9; 13 CFR 124.520 (8(a) Participants); 13 CFR 121.103(b)(6) (affiliation exception); 13 CFR 125.10 (other agencies' programs)
what: Under SBA's Mentor-Protégé Program a for-profit mentor of any size assists a small protégé under a written agreement that SBA approves (15 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 657r; 13 CFR 125.9) [787](#cite:787) [785](#cite:785). "A [joint venture](#term:joint-venture) between a protégé and its mentor will qualify as a small business for any procurement for which the protégé individually qualifies as small." (13 CFR 125.9(d)(1)) [785](#cite:785). The [8(a)](#term:eight-a) and All Small mentor-protégé programs were merged into this single program on November 16, 2020 [782](#cite:782) [791](#cite:791).
who_for: Protégé: a firm that is small in its primary [NAICS code](#term:naics), or in a secondary code where it has experience, and has already found a mentor. Mentor: a for-profit firm of any size.
how_it_works: Application: through [certify.sba.gov](#term:mysba-certifications); MySBA Certifications handles contracting certifications but mentor-protégé applications stay on certify.sba.gov [788](#cite:788) [790](#cite:790)
Processing: "15 days screening plus 90 days processing (if your application is not withdrawn), totaling 105 days." [788](#cite:788)
If SBA declines the agreement, the firm may not reapply with the same mentor for 60 calendar days (13 CFR 125.9(f)) [785](#cite:785)

Annual reporting: within 30 days of each anniversary the protégé reports assistance received, loans and equity, [subcontracts](#term:prime-and-subcontractor), joint venture contracts and a narrative, and certifies any change in terms; SBA may decline continuation where assistance was not provided or yielded no material benefit (13 CFR 125.9(g)) [785](#cite:785)

A mentor found not to have provided the assistance has 30 days to respond; SBA then terminates the agreement, bars the firm as a mentor for two years, may recommend stop-work orders on joint venture contracts and may treat it as grounds for [debarment](#term:responsibility) (13 CFR 125.9(h)) [785](#cite:785)
SBA publishes the list of active agreements as an Excel file (effective July 7, 2026); the page states no count [793](#cite:793)

Other agencies' programs need SBA approval; DoD's program and [SBIR](#term:sbir)/[STTR](#term:sttr) mentoring are exempt (15 U.S.C. 657r(b); 13 CFR 125.10) [787](#cite:787) [786](#cite:786). [GAO](#term:gao) counted 13 agency programs in 2011 [826](#cite:826). Programs with a live page have their own records here: [NASA](#term:agency-abbreviations), DOE, DOT, Treasury and FAA

GSA: no separate program; [GSAR](#term:gsar) subpart 519.70 and [clauses](#term:clause-numbering) 552.219-75 and 552.219-76 were removed effective April 3, 2019 and firms use SBA's program [815](#cite:815)

VA: no separate codified program; VAAR subpart 819.71 displays as "[Reserved]" [823](#cite:823) and VA's September 2019 brief refers firms to SBA-approved relationships under 13 CFR 125.9 [824](#cite:824)

DHS: status conflicting; the page body says [OSDBU](#term:osdbu) will not accept new applications from March 1, 2023 until further notice, while the page's search-result title says the program relaunched and a May 2025 program guide exists but could not be read [811](#cite:811)

State and HHS: codified only (DOSAR 619.202-70; HHSAR 352.219-70 and 319.270-1); no live program page was read for either [818](#cite:818) [821](#cite:821). EPA: no formal program page; its Office of Small Business Programs suggests partners for "mentor/protege relationships" [825](#cite:825)
benefits: A joint venture with the mentor counts as small wherever the protégé alone is small (13 CFR 125.9(d)(1)) [785](#cite:785)
No affiliation or control is found solely on the basis of the agreement or the assistance given under it (13 CFR 125.9(d)(4); 121.103(b)(6)) [785](#cite:785) [770](#cite:770)
The mentor may own up to 40% of the protégé (13 CFR 125.9(d)(2)) [785](#cite:785)
The protégé has a right of first refusal on the mentor's interest in the joint venture [785](#cite:785)
Assistance areas: management and technical; financial; contracting; international trade; business development; general and administrative [791](#cite:791)
An 8(a) Participant may take part like any other small business; its joint venture with the mentor on 8(a) contracts must meet 13 CFR 124.513(c) and (d) [775](#cite:775)
requirements: Mentor: a for-profit concern of any size with good character and a favourable financial position, not debarred or suspended (13 CFR 125.9(b)) [785](#cite:785); SBA's page says for-profit or agricultural cooperative [788](#cite:788)

Mentor's limit: generally no more than three protégés at one time, counting parent and subsidiaries in aggregate; the first two relationships with Puerto Rico-based small businesses do not count (13 CFR 125.9(b)(3)) [785](#cite:785)

Protégé: small for its primary NAICS code, or a secondary code in which it has prior experience (13 CFR 125.9(c)(1)) [785](#cite:785); SBA's page adds for-profit or agricultural cooperative, with a proposed mentor before applying [788](#cite:788)

Protégé's limits: generally one mentor at a time, with a second only where SBA approves it as not competing or conflicting (13 CFR 125.9(c)(2)); generally two mentor-protégé agreements with different mentors in total, and no more than 12 years in total as a protégé (13 CFR 125.9(c)(4)) [785](#cite:785)

Agreement: written, with a needs assessment, the assistance and a timeline, and a single point of contact; the mentor commits for at least one year; either party may terminate on 30 days' notice; "The term of a mentor-protégé agreement may not exceed six years."; SBA must approve changes (13 CFR 125.9(e)) [785](#cite:785)
steps: Find a mentor first: "Have a proposed mentor prior to applying for the program" [790](#cite:790)
Register both firms in [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov); the protégé's [UEI](#term:uei) is needed [788](#cite:788)
Both firms complete SBA's online tutorial at learn.sba.gov/sba-mpp and keep the training certificates [788](#cite:788) [790](#cite:790)
Write and sign the Mentor-Protégé Agreement; SBA posts a template (the page is on legacy.sba.gov) [792](#cite:792)

Apply at certify.sba.gov, uploading the signed agreement, both training certificates, copies of any active SBA or other-agency mentor-protégé agreements, an SBA size redetermination letter if applicable, and proof of experience when applying under a secondary NAICS code [790](#cite:790)
Allow 105 days [788](#cite:788)
Report every year within 30 days of the anniversary [785](#cite:785); SBA's mailboxes are sbampp@sba.gov, mppjvreporting@sba.gov and mppevaluations@sba.gov [788](#cite:788)

Stale regulatory text: DFARS Appendix I-103 as displayed (DFARS Change 05/07/2026) ties credit or reimbursement to mentors "incurring costs through September 30, 2026", a date now passed, while the statute is permanent; the headings of Appendix I and subpart 219.71 still say "Pilot" [450](#cite:450) [795](#cite:795) [451](#cite:451). Whether a DFARS case is open to remove the date was not established.

L. 119-60, December 18, 2025) come from a secondary source [807](#cite:807); the govinfo text was truncated and showed no mention of the program in the portion read [806](#cite:806); the LII copy of the statute shows no amendment after December 23, 2024 [451](#cite:451).

name: DoD Mentor-Protégé Program
governing_text: 10 U.S.C. 4902; DFARS subpart 219.71; DFARS Appendix I; DFARS 252.219-7003(c); exempt from SBA approval under 13 CFR 125.10(c)
what: The [DoD Mentor-Protégé Program](#term:mentor-protege-dod) is established by 10 U.S.C. 4902 and implemented by DFARS subpart 219.71 and Appendix I [451](#cite:451) [795](#cite:795). A mentor is reimbursed for developmental assistance to a [protégé](#term:mentor-protege-sba), capped at $1,000,000 per protégé per fiscal year unless unusual circumstances are found, or takes credit toward its subcontracting goals at four, three or two times the cost [451]. Section 856 of Pub. L. 117-263 (December 23, 2022) made the program permanent and cut the mentor threshold from $100 million to $25 million [451](#cite:451).
who_for: Protégé: a small firm in one of the statute's eight categories. Mentor: a DoD contractor with $25,000,000 in prior-year DoD contracts or otherwise approved, typically a prime with an active [subcontracting plan](#term:subcontracting-plan).
how_it_works: Who approves: the Mentor-Protégé Program Director in OSD's [Office of Small Business Programs](#term:osdbu) approves mentors; component OSBP directors approve agreements; DCMA conducts annual performance reviews (DFARS 219.7103-1, 219.7106) [795](#cite:795)
DoD's program is exempt from the [SBA](#term:sba) approval that other agencies' mentor-protégé programs need (13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 125.10(c)) [786](#cite:786)
Two tracks: direct-reimbursed agreements go to the defense agency OSBP and start when funds are obligated; credit agreements go to DCMA and start on approval [798](#cite:798)

The mentor submits its prior approval, the signed agreement, the credit-or-reimbursement election, the estimated annual cost and a justification for reimbursable costs above $1 million a year; approval is needed before costs are incurred (Appendix I-108); incidental expenses may run to 10 percent of total estimated cost (I-109) [450]; no reimbursement above $1 million in a [fiscal year](#term:fiscal-year) per protégé without a written determination (DFARS 219.7103-2) [795](#cite:795)

Component routes: Army uses a white paper with a program manager's endorsement, then an invitation-only [RFP](#term:solicitation), and offers reimbursable, credit and hybrid agreements [800](#cite:800); Air Force runs a [Broad Agency Announcement](#term:baa) in which only mentors submit a white paper and then a three-volume proposal [801](#cite:801); DTRA takes white papers at any time under Notice ID HDTRA124S0001 [803](#cite:803); DLA's OSBP does not pair mentors and protégés [802](#cite:802); NGA reports 14 active agreements and a plan to reach 20 during FY2025-FY2026 [804](#cite:804)
Size of the program: DoD's paperwork notice counts 96 respondents and 180 annual responses [797](#cite:797)
Nunn-Perry Awards for outstanding mentor-protégé teams were announced April 9, 2026: five teams for FY2024 and three for FY2025 [799](#cite:799)
benefits: Protégé: personnel help in management, engineering and technical matters; noncompetitive [subcontracts](#term:prime-and-subcontractor); progress and advance payments; loans; assistance obtained from [SBDCs](#term:sbdc), procurement technical assistance entities, HBCUs and minority institutions, and [women's business centers](#term:wbc) (10 U.S.C. 4902(f)) [451](#cite:451)

Mentor: reimbursement through a separately priced contract line item or separate contract, or credit at four times (third-party assistance), three times (mentor employees) and two times (other costs) (10 U.S.C. 4902(g); Appendix I-103, I-110) [451](#cite:451) [450](#cite:450); mentor firms may count awards to protégés toward [small disadvantaged business](#term:sdb) goals (DFARS 252.219-7003(c)) [718](#cite:718)
DoD says it has supported more than 190 small businesses over the past five years [111](#cite:111)
requirements: Mentor: $25,000,000 in DoD contracts in the fiscal year before the agreement, or otherwise approved; no agreement if SBA finds the firms affiliated (10 U.S.C. 4902(d)) [451]. Appendix I-102(a): eligible for federal contracts, in good financial health and character, not debarred, other than small unless approved, showing capability by $25 million in prior-year DoD contracts or subcontracts, an active subcontracting plan as a DoD prime, 8(a) graduate status, or Director approval [450](#cite:450)
DoD's how-to page and the Air Force page say the mentor must be performing under at least one active approved subcontracting plan [798](#cite:798) [801](#cite:801)

Protégé categories in the statute: socially and economically disadvantaged; Indian tribe-owned; Native Hawaiian Organization-owned; qualified organization employing the severely disabled; women-owned; service-disabled veteran-owned; HUBZone; nontraditional defense contractor or supplier of critical goods or services [451](#cite:451). Appendix I-102(b): small, not above the SBA size standard for its primary NAICS code, and not owned or managed by holders of stock options or convertible securities in the mentor [450](#cite:450)

"A protege firm may not be a party to more than one DoD mentor-protege agreement at a time." [450](#cite:450); protégé authority runs for 5 years from its first agreement (10 U.S.C. 4902(c)) [451](#cite:451)

Term: not more than three years, up to five if the Secretary finds unusual circumstances (10 U.S.C. 4902(e)) [451](#cite:451); DFARS Case 2023-D011 set an initial three years extendable by up to two more with OSBP Director approval [796](#cite:796)
The mentor alone selects the protégé (Appendix I-104) and cannot require a protégé agreement as a condition of a subcontract (I-106) [450](#cite:450)

Reporting (Appendix I-112): mentors semiannually for periods ending March 31 and September 30, due 30 days after; protégés annually by October 31 during the agreement and for 2 fiscal years after [450](#cite:450)
steps: Find a counterpart: "Mentors and Protégés are solely responsible for finding their counterpart" [798](#cite:798)
Choose direct-reimbursed or credit [798](#cite:798)
Develop the agreement from a needs assessment [798](#cite:798)
Submit: reimbursed agreements to the defense agency OSBP, credit agreements to DCMA [798](#cite:798)
Start: credit agreements on approval, reimbursed agreements when funds are obligated [798](#cite:798)
Report semiannually, with annual DCMA reviews and protégé reports for two years after [798](#cite:798)
Questions to dodmpp@osd.mil or 571-372-6191 [798](#cite:798) [111](#cite:111)

name: Prototype other transaction (10 U.S.C. 4022)
governing_text: 10 U.S.C. 4022 (as amended through Pub. L. 119-60); 10 U.S.C. 3014 (nontraditional defense contractor); 32 CFR Part 3 (out of step with the statute); DoD Other Transactions Guide, Version 2.0 (July 2023); USD(A&S) memorandum of August 27, 2025 (approval authority)
what: A prototype other transaction (OT) is a legally binding instrument other than a standard [procurement contract](#term:grant), grant, or cooperative agreement, used by DoD to carry out a prototype project under 10 U.S.C. 4022 [1053](#cite:1053) [1028](#cite:1028). The [FAR](#term:far) and many standard procurement contract requirements do not automatically apply; the Procurement Integrity Act and fiscal law still do [1053](#cite:1053). A "prototype project" includes a proof of concept, model, or process (including a business process); reverse engineering to address obsolescence; a pilot or novel application of commercial technologies for defense purposes; agile development activity; the creation, design, development, or demonstration of operational utility; or any combination [1029](#cite:1029) [1059](#cite:1059).
who_for: The DARPA Director, the [DIU](#term:diu) Director, the Secretary of a military department, or any other official designated by the Secretary of Defense may carry out prototype projects [1028](#cite:1028). Any firm can take part, and the statutory conditions favour [nontraditional defense contractors](#term:nontraditional-defense-contractor) and small businesses: a project needs no [cost share](#term:cost-share) when at least one nontraditional defense contractor or [nonprofit research institution](#term:sttr) participates to a significant extent, or when all significant participants are small businesses or nontraditional defense contractors [1028](#cite:1028).
how_it_works: One of four conditions must be met (10 U.S.C. 4022(d)(1)): (A) at least one nontraditional defense contractor or nonprofit research institution participating to a significant extent; (B) all significant participants other than the Federal Government are small businesses (including [SBIR](#term:sbir)/STTR participants under 15 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 638) or nontraditional defense contractors; (C) at least one third of the total cost paid from non-Federal sources; (D) the agency senior procurement executive determines in writing that exceptional circumstances justify the transaction [1028](#cite:1028)

In the statute "small business" means a [small business concern](#term:size-standard) under section 3 of the [Small Business Act](#term:small-business-act) (15 U.S.C. 632), and "nontraditional defense contractor" has the meaning given in 10 U.S.C. 3014 [1029](#cite:1029) [1054](#cite:1054)

Costs incurred before the transaction's effective date do not count toward cost share, except costs incurred after negotiations began, on a written determination by the responsible official (4022(d)(2)) [1028](#cite:1028)

"Significant extent", in DoD's superseded 2018 guide: the [Agreements Officer](#term:contracting-officer) judges the totality of the circumstances; examples are supplying a new key technology, product or process; a novel application; a material increase in performance, efficiency, quality or versatility; accomplishing a significant amount of the project; or a material reduction in cost or schedule; "AOs should not establish blanket rules or thresholds for determination of significance" [1050](#cite:1050). The July 2023 guide gives no definition of "significant extent" in the portion read [1049](#cite:1049)

Competition: "To the maximum extent practicable, competitive procedures shall be used when entering into agreements to carry out the prototype projects under subsection (a)." [1028](#cite:1028); "Although the Competition in Contracting Act does not apply to OTs, competition should be pursued to the maximum extent practicable." [1054](#cite:1054)
The [Inspector General](#term:dod-ig) restated the point in 2023: "the DoD is required to use competitive procedures to the maximum extent practicable to award OT agreements." [1126](#cite:1126)
Evaluation: the FAR, the [DFARS](#term:dfars), DoD Source Selection Procedures and the Competition in Contracting Act do not apply to OT evaluation [1049](#cite:1049)

Guidance in force: WARU's guide page lists July 2023 as the current edition of the OT Guide, issued by OUSD(A&S), shows no newer one, and links the companion Guide to Research Other Transactions [1051](#cite:1051)
Advertising: DoD's guide says [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) "may not be the most appropriate place" to advertise OT opportunities [1049](#cite:1049)

Ways the opportunity reaches firms: a [commercial solutions opening](#term:cso) structured to award prototype OTs [1058](#cite:1058), or a request issued to the members of a [consortium](#term:consortium) through its [management organization](#term:consortium-manager) [1119](#cite:1119); see routes defense-commercial-solutions-opening and ot-consortium-membership

Payment may be [fixed-price](#term:firm-fixed-price), expenditure-based, payable-milestone, or hybrid [1053](#cite:1053); DARPA's training says advance payments are permitted and milestone-based methods are used [1063](#cite:1063)

Approval (statute): over $100,000,000 but not over $500,000,000 (including all options), a written determination by the head of the contracting activity (or the director, for DARPA, DIU, MDA); over $500,000,000, a written determination by the senior procurement executive (or DARPA/DIU/MDA director) and written notice to the congressional defense committees at least 30 days before the authority is exercised; the determination authority may not be delegated [1028](#cite:1028). Still applies: criminal laws (false claims, false statements); laws of general applicability (Civil Rights Act); laws applicable to U.S. business (environmental, import/export control); Procurement Integrity Act (41 U.S.C. 2102–07) [1063](#cite:1063). ARPA-H's list adds the Antideficiency Act, the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act, NEPA, [debarment](#term:responsibility) and suspension, and research misconduct and human subjects protections [1066](#cite:1066). DoD's guide adds FOIA with the five-year protection of [10 U.S.C. 4021](#term:research-ot)(i), classified-information rules (32 CFR Part 117), [DoDI](#term:dodi-5000-02) 5200.48 for [CUI](#term:fci-cui), and [section 889](#term:section-889) of the FY2019 NDAA [1049](#cite:1049)
Fiscal law governs OTs: GAO applied the recording statute and the bona fide needs statute to [NIH](#term:agency-abbreviations) other transactions (B-333150, April 8, 2024) [1077](#cite:1077)

A prototype OT may provide for the award of a [follow-on production contract](#term:follow-on-production) or transaction to the participants [1029](#cite:1029) [1054](#cite:1054); see route follow-on-production-ot

What a small firm must have: the sweep found no certification prescribed by section 4022; a firm that is a small business or a nontraditional defense contractor meets condition (A) or (B) without cost share [1028](#cite:1028). See certification nontraditional-defense-contractor

Registration: "each member serving as the primary performer on an award must obtain a [Unique Entity Identifier](#term:uei) (UEI) from SAM." [1049](#cite:1049). In Independent Rough Terrain Center the protester's SAM registration lapsed between May 26 and August 9, 2023, after proposal submission and before award, and its protest was dismissed [1083](#cite:1083)

Scale: DoD obligations through prototype and production OTAs grew from $1.8 billion in fiscal year 2016 to over $18 billion in fiscal year 2024; prototype OTAs were $56.3 billion of $62.9 billion obligated in FY2021–FY2024 (90 percent) [1070](#cite:1070)

Who takes part: companies that typically did not do business with DoD "participated to a significant extent on 88 percent of the transactions awarded during this time" (FY2016–FY2018) [1072](#cite:1072)

Policy direction: the November 2025 [Acquisition Transformation Strategy](#term:warfighting-acquisition-system) says the Department "will direct the use of the other transaction authority (OTA) for prototype and follow-on production efforts" where in the best interest of the warfighter, and commits to "increase engagement with nontraditional defense contractors to educate industry on how to compete for OTAs" [1062](#cite:1062)
Installation and facility prototyping pilot (4022(i)): two projects a year, $300,000,000 aggregate, ends September 30, 2030 [1028](#cite:1028)

conflicts: Edition: the guide read is "revised July 2025" (WARU-hosted copy) [1052](#cite:1052); the ARPA-H policy library lists a Research OT Guide (Sep 2023) [1068](#cite:1068).
name: Research other transaction (10 U.S.C. 4021)
governing_text: 10 U.S.C. 4021; Guide to Research Other Transactions Under 10 U.S.C. 4021 (OUSD(R&E), revised July 2025); 32 CFR Part 37 (Technology Investment Agreements)
what: The Secretary of Defense and each military department Secretary "may enter into transactions (other than contracts, [cooperative agreements](#term:grant), and grants) under the authority of this subsection" in carrying out basic, applied, and advanced research projects [1031](#cite:1031) [1030](#cite:1030). [Research OTs](#term:research-ot) are focused on validating research results rather than delivering the resulting technology [1052](#cite:1052). They "do not include authority for [follow-on production](#term:follow-on-production) contracts or transactions" [1055](#cite:1055).
who_for: Performers of basic, applied and advanced research who can share the cost [1052](#cite:1052). Statutory award authority sits with the Secretary of Defense, the military department Secretaries and DARPA; others need delegation [1052](#cite:1052). The Secretary of Defense acts through DARPA, [DIU](#term:diu), or any other DoD element the Secretary designates; the Defense Innovation Unit was added by [Pub. L.](#term:public-law) 118-31, section 913(a)(2) (Dec. 22, 2023) [1031](#cite:1031) [1030](#cite:1030).
how_it_works: Conditions (4021(e)): the Secretary must ensure, to the maximum extent practicable, no duplication of research under existing DoD programs, and, to the extent the Secretary determines practicable, that Government funds do not exceed the total provided by other parties [1031](#cite:1031) [1055](#cite:1055)

Resource share is required and, to the maximum extent practicable, Government funds do not exceed the total provided by the other parties [1052](#cite:1052); DARPA's training says [cost share](#term:cost-share) 50/50 is preferred for research [1063](#cite:1063)
Advance payments: "The authority provided under subsection (a) may be exercised without regard to section 3324 of title 31." [1030](#cite:1030)
Proposals, business plans and technical information submitted are protected from disclosure for five years after receipt (4021(i)) [1030](#cite:1030)
A research OT structured as an assistance transaction may be a Technology Investment Agreement under 32 [CFR](#term:cfr) Part 37 [1055](#cite:1055)
A [Comptroller General](#term:gao) access [clause](#term:clause-numbering) is not required for Research OTs [1049](#cite:1049)

Still applicable: fiscal laws, regulations and policies; [suspension and debarment](#term:responsibility); lobbying restrictions; criminal statutes; export laws; industrial security. Not applicable: the Competition in Contracting Act and the DoD Grants and Agreements Regulations [1052](#cite:1052)
"Laws and regulations of general applicability or unrelated to the award process will generally still apply to Research OTs" [1052](#cite:1052)

IP: "[OTs](#term:other-transaction) are not subject to the statutory regimes of the Bayh-Dole Act (35 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 201-212) for patentable inventions or 10 U.S.C. 3771 for technical data"; IP rights are fully negotiable [1052](#cite:1052)
Disputes: agreements should set out how either party raises a dispute and favor alternative dispute resolution [1052](#cite:1052)
Within [consortia](#term:consortium) the research form is rare: of $24,337.9 million obligated on consortia-based OTAs in FY2019–2021, research was $34.6 million [1119](#cite:1119)

What a small firm must have: resource share, with Government funds not exceeding the other parties' total to the extent practicable [1052](#cite:1052); the sweep found no certification prescribed [1055](#cite:1055)

pending_changes.text: DoD's [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) for 32 [CFR](#term:cfr) Part 3 says [follow-on production](#term:follow-on-production) for a [consortium](#term:consortium) subproject "is not contingent upon the successful completion of all activities within a consortium."; final status not checked [1130](#cite:1130).

conflicts: Notice of a possible follow-on: DoD guidance says the solicitation and the agreement must or should give it [1059](#cite:1059) [1049](#cite:1049); the statute allows the award "even if explicit notification was not listed within the request for proposal for the transaction" [1029](#cite:1029).

GAO-25-107546 figures: an earlier pass of the fetch tool returned "production OTA use increased from $24 million (FY2021) to $450 million (FY2024)", which conflicts with GAO's "$2 billion in production OTA use in fiscal year 2024"; treated as an extraction error until rechecked [1070](#cite:1070).
name: Follow-on production after a prototype OT (10 U.S.C. 4022(f))
governing_text: 10 U.S.C. 4022(f) and 4022(a)(2)(C); DoD Other Transactions Guide, Version 2.0 (July 2023); USD(A&S) memorandum of August 27, 2025
what: A follow-on production contract or transaction is one to produce, sustain, or otherwise implement the results of a successfully completed [prototype project](#term:prototype-ot) for continued or expanded use by DoD, and it may be awarded to the prototype participants without further competition [1029](#cite:1029) [1054](#cite:1054). [DIU](#term:diu) puts it this way: a competitively awarded prototype OT "may result in the award of a follow-on production contract or agreement without the use of additional competitive procedures" [97](#cite:97). DoD's guide names Production OTs under 10 U.S.C. 4022(f) as one of three [OT](#term:other-transaction) types [1049](#cite:1049).
who_for: Participants in a prototype OT that was competitively awarded and successfully completed [1029](#cite:1029) [1054](#cite:1054).
how_it_works: Two conditions (4022(f)(2)): "competitive procedures were used for the selection of parties for participation in the transaction" and "the participants in the transaction successfully completed the prototype project provided for in the transaction" [1029](#cite:1029) [1054](#cite:1054)

Notice: the statute as now in force allows the follow-on award "even if explicit notification was not listed within the request for proposal for the transaction" [1029](#cite:1029); it was amended after [GAO](#term:gao) sustained a 2018 [protest](#term:bid-protest) in which the prototype agreement had no follow-on provision [1074](#cite:1074). DoD's 2018 memo says [solicitation](#term:solicitation) documents and prototype agreements must include notice of potential follow-on production OTs [1059](#cite:1059), and the July 2023 guide says the solicitation and the Prototype OT agreement should include it [1049](#cite:1049)

"Successfully completed" means the performer met the key technical goals, satisfied the success metrics in the Prototype OT, or accomplished a particularly favorable or unexpected result [1049](#cite:1049); successful completion requires a written determination [1059](#cite:1059); it can occur before the whole prototype project ends, so that a useful part can move to production [1050](#cite:1050)

Consortia: a follow-on may be awarded when DoD determines that an individual prototype or prototype subproject within a consortium is successfully completed; it is not contingent on completion of all consortium activities (4022(f)(3)) [1029](#cite:1029) [1130](#cite:1130)

Form: follow-on awards may be made under 4022(a), under chapter 137, or under procedures the Secretary establishes by regulation (4022(f)(5)), so the follow-on may be an OT or a [FAR](#term:far) contract [1029](#cite:1029) [97](#cite:97)

Approval: a follow-on production contract or transaction over $100,000,000 (including all options) needs a covered official's written determination that (d) was met for the prior prototype transaction, that (f) will be met, and that use is essential to meet critical national security objectives, with the congressional defense committees notified at the time the authority is exercised [1028](#cite:1028) [1060](#cite:1060)

Who approves in DoD: service acquisition executive (military departments); Director (DARPA/DIU/MDA); for defense agencies and combatant commands, Director or commanding officer up to $100M and USD(R&E) or USD(A&S) above [1060](#cite:1060)
A Comptroller General access [clause](#term:clause-numbering) is required for Prototype or follow-on production OTs with payments over $5 million [1049](#cite:1049)
Prototypes or follow-on items may be provided to another contractor as Government-furnished equipment (4022(g)) [1028](#cite:1028)

GAO sustained one protest on this route: in Oracle America (B-416061, May 31, 2018) "the Army did not properly exercise the authority granted to it under the statute", because the prototype OTA had no follow-on provision and the prototype project was not complete at award [1074](#cite:1074)
The Court of Federal Claims has held that "nothing in the OT statutes expressly removes OT follow-on contracts from the purview of this Court's jurisdiction" [1083](#cite:1083)

In practice: production OTA use was $2 billion in [fiscal year](#term:fiscal-year) 2024; ten of 18 weapon-system efforts GAO reviewed have awarded or plan FAR contracts for further development and testing before FAR production; DoD's manual reporting named 48 FAR production contracts using follow-on authority and only seven (15 percent) actually were [1070](#cite:1070)

Within consortia: "Nearly all consortia-based OTA obligations were through prototype OTAs rather than production OTAs." [1122](#cite:1122); NAMC says its GVS OTA allows follow-on production [1231](#cite:1231); ATI describes MATAC's OTA as for prototyping and production [1210](#cite:1210)
[Research OTs](#term:research-ot) carry no follow-on production authority [1055](#cite:1055)

Under the amended [CSO](#term:cso) statute a product, service or item acquired through a commercial solutions opening may also lead to a follow-on production contract or transaction as defined in section 4022 [1033](#cite:1033) [806](#cite:806)

What a small firm must have: a prototype OT that was competitively awarded and successfully completed [1029](#cite:1029) [1054](#cite:1054); a [SAM registration](#term:sam-gov) that stays active through award, since a lapse ended one protester's case [1083](#cite:1083)

pending_changes.text: [Pub. L. 119-60](#term:ndaa), section 1823 (Dec. 18, 2025, 139 Stat. 1247) removed "innovative" from 10 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 3458(a), added [nondevelopmental items](#term:commercial-product) and the technical/operational review options, added [follow-on production](#term:follow-on-production) in (c), struck the former definition of "innovative" and removed the prior approval requirement; there is no separate effective-date note [1033](#cite:1033) [806](#cite:806). Codified [DFARS](#term:dfars) Subpart 212.70 (DFARS Change 05/07/2026) still covers only "innovative commercial products or commercial services" and still requires senior procurement executive approval to award a contract in excess of $100 million (212.7003); no deviation notice appears on the page [1040](#cite:1040). No DFARS implementation of section 1823 was found as of 2026-10-03 [1040](#cite:1040) [1048](#cite:1048).

DoD [class deviation](#term:class-deviation) 2026-O0028 ([Revolutionary FAR Overhaul](#term:revolutionary-far-overhaul) [Part 12](#term:far-part-12), DFARS Part 212), effective February 1, 2026 and issued December 18, 2025 per a law-firm tracker, keeps Subpart 212.70: 212.7000–212.7002 retain "innovative commercial products or commercial services" and [fixed-price](#term:firm-fixed-price) type contracts, and 212.7004(e) carries the [Certificate of Competency](#term:responsibility) step [1046](#cite:1046) [1048](#cite:1048). It does not reflect section 1823 [1046](#cite:1046).

FAR overhaul: the overhauled FAR Part 12 model deviation text (page last updated 2026-09-28) has no "[commercial solutions opening](#term:cso)" section or term in the text read; 12.201-1 covers [simplified procedures](#term:simplified-acquisition-procedures) up to $9 million (or $15 million in specified circumstances) and 12.201-2 covers larger acquisitions [395](#cite:395).

conflicts: Statute vs regulation: 10 U.S.C. 3458(a) as amended no longer says "innovative" [1033](#cite:1033); codified DFARS 212.7000 and class deviation 2026-O0028 still do [1040](#cite:1040) [1046](#cite:1046); the AAF CSO page and the Acquipedia article do not mention the change [1056](#cite:1056) [1058](#cite:1058). The section heading on the LII page itself still contains "innovative" [1033](#cite:1033).

Approval above $100 million: the pre-amendment statute required a written determination of efficacy by USD(A&S) [1034](#cite:1034); DFARS 212.7003 and the AAF CSO page say senior procurement executive approval [1040](#cite:1040) [1056](#cite:1056); the AAF BAA-v-CSO page says USD(A&S) or service acquisition executive approval [1057](#cite:1057); the amended statute as read on LII removed the prior approval requirement [1033](#cite:1033).

Authority cited: the AAF BAA-v-CSO page gives section 879 of the FY2017 NDAA and describes the CSO as for innovative commercial items [1057](#cite:1057); the final rule implements section 803 of the FY2022 NDAA (Pub. L. 117-81) and section 814 of the FY2023 NDAA (Pub. L. 117-263) [1042](#cite:1042).
Federal Register page: the final rule is recorded as 88 FR 55937 [1042](#cite:1042); eCFR gives the subpart's source as 88 FR 55939, Aug. 17, 2023 [1041](#cite:1041).

Secondary only: law-firm commentary describes section 1823 as expanding CSO authority to any commercial product or service and creating sole-source follow-on production authority [1108](#cite:1108) [1111](#cite:1111) [1112](#cite:1112); one explainer puts the removed written determination at "$10 million", which appears to be a slip for $100 million [1112](#cite:1112) vs [1034](#cite:1034).
name: Commercial Solutions Opening, defense (10 U.S.C. 3458; DFARS 212.70)
governing_text: 10 U.S.C. 3458 as amended by Pub. L. 119-60, section 1823 (Dec. 18, 2025, 139 Stat. 1247); DFARS Subpart 212.70 (88 FR 55937, Aug. 17, 2023; not yet conformed to the amendment); for CSOs that award prototype OTs, 10 U.S.C. 4022
what: A commercial solutions opening (CSO) is a general [solicitation](#term:solicitation) under which the Secretary of Defense and each military department Secretary "may acquire commercial products, commercial services, or nondevelopmental items through a competitive selection of proposals resulting from a general solicitation" and a peer review, technical review, or operational review [1033](#cite:1033) [806](#cite:806). Until Pub. L. 119-60, section 1823 (enacted December 18, 2025) the authority was to "acquire innovative commercial products and commercial services through a competitive selection of proposals" [1034](#cite:1034) [806](#cite:806). The name covers two authorities: CSOs "may be structured as [prototype OTs](#term:prototype-ot) pursuant to 10 U.S.C. 4022, or as FAR-based contracts or agreements pursuant to 10 U.S.C. 3458/DFARS 212.70" [1058](#cite:1058).
who_for: Firms with commercial or near-commercial solutions: WARU's Acquipedia article describes a CSO loosely as "a [BAA](#term:baa) for higher TRL items" [1058](#cite:1058). In the FY2018–FY2022 pilot, 120 contracts were awarded from CSOs, 82 (68%) to small entities, 72 unique small entities [1042](#cite:1042).
how_it_works: Lifecycle: a CSO is a long-duration solicitation (typically one or more years) seeking solutions to Government-specified problems known as "areas of interest". CSO posted; area of interest posted; industry submits short-form responses; Government reviews against stated factors; award decisions; areas of interest updated, added or deleted; CSO closed [1058](#cite:1058)

Codified procedure (DFARS 212.7004): the CSO describes the agency's interest, evaluation factors, proposal period and instructions; technical merit and importance to agency programs are the primary evaluation factors; it is publicized through the [Governmentwide point of entry](#term:sam-gov); proposals are evaluated by scientific, technological or other subject-matter expert peer review; no separate [FAR](#term:far) 5.2 [synopsis](#term:synopsis) for individual awards [1040](#cite:1040)
"Proposals need not be evaluated against each other since they are not submitted in response to a common performance work statement" [1042](#cite:1042)
The subpart has six sections: 212.7000 Scope; 212.7001 Definition; 212.7002 Policy; 212.7003 Limitations; 212.7004 Procedures; 212.7005 Congressional notification [1041](#cite:1041)
Used when meaningful proposals with varying technical or scientific approaches can be reasonably anticipated (DFARS 212.7002) [1040](#cite:1040)

Award under section 3458: "Contracts or agreements entered into using the authority under subsection (a) shall be fixed-price, including fixed-price incentive contracts."; products and services acquired are treated as commercial products and commercial services [1033](#cite:1033) [1040](#cite:1040)
Use of general solicitation competitive procedures counts as use of competitive procedures for chapter 221 (3458(b)) [1033](#cite:1033) [1056](#cite:1056)

Follow-on production (new in section 1823): for a product, service, or item acquired under a CSO the Secretary may enter into "a follow-on production contract (including a [sole source](#term:sole-source) contract), subject to the approval requirements of section 3204(e) of this title", or a follow-on production contract or transaction as defined in section 4022 [1033](#cite:1033) [806](#cite:806)
Congressional notification within 45 days of award for contracts exceeding $100,000,000 (3458(e)) [1033](#cite:1033) [1040](#cite:1040)

[DIU](#term:diu)'s CSO, which awards prototype OTs: step 1, the company sends a short brief about its solution; step 2, DIU invites selected companies to pitch; step 3, proposal and award. Awards are prototype agreements under [OT](#term:other-transaction) authority (10 U.S.C. 4022), "in as few as 60-90 days" [97](#cite:97)

DIU solution brief: "Solution Briefs not exceed 5 written pages using 12-point font or 15 briefing slides."; content is company name and history, employee count, [CAGE code](#term:cage-code) or [UEI](#term:uei) if applicable, financing stage; technology in production now; a response to each requirement in the Area of Interest [1065](#cite:1065)

DIU Phase 2 pitch factors: relevance to the Area of Interest; technical merit and feasibility; company viability; innovation or uniqueness; rough-order-of-magnitude pricing; notional schedule; [data rights](#term:sbir-data-rights) implications [1065](#cite:1065)
DIU states that companies retain ownership of IP assets created during the effort [97](#cite:97)

Compared with a BAA: "CSO procedures are similar to Broad Agency Announcement procedures, but CSOs are broader" [1056](#cite:1056); a BAA is for basic and applied research and development not related to a specific system or hardware requirement and "Cannot be used for production" [1057](#cite:1057). See route baa-far-35-016

Compared with a [consortium](#term:consortium) request: a CSO is publicized through the Governmentwide point of entry [1040](#cite:1040); for most consortia, "members pay dues to join the consortium and gain exclusive access to government opportunities" [1071](#cite:1071)
Awards are fixed-price FAR contracts or, when separately authorized, agreements [1056](#cite:1056)

Small-business responsibility: under DoD's Part 212 deviation text, if a small business would be selected but is found not responsible, the [SBA](#term:sba) Certificate of Competency procedure is followed (212.7004(e)) [1046](#cite:1046)

Software: a Secretary of Defense memo of March 6, 2025 directs "Commercial Solutions Openings and Other Transactions as the default solicitation and award approaches for acquiring capabilities under the [SWP](#term:software-acquisition-pathway)" [1061](#cite:1061)

Combatant commands: a statutory note ([Pub. L.](#term:public-law) 118-31, section 813) requires the Secretary to use section 3458 at least four times a year for geographic combatant command needs, through September 30, 2027 [1033](#cite:1033)

[Protest](#term:bid-protest): the Court of Federal Claims took jurisdiction over a CSO that awarded an [IDIQ](#term:idiq) contract (Kinemetrics, Inc. v. United States, 155 Fed. Cl. 777 (2021)) [1080](#cite:1080)
Small-business record: FY2020, FY2021 and FY2022 each saw 19 unique small entities awarded a CSO contract [1042](#cite:1042)
Civilian agencies: the overhauled FAR Part 12 text read contains no CSO procedure [395](#cite:395); civilian CSO authority was not swept, so there is no civilian CSO route in this slice (todo)
Further resources linked from the [AAF](#term:aaf) page: [AFWERX](#term:afwerx) CSO resources, DIU CSO process video, [GSA](#term:gsa) Procurement Innovation Resource Center [1056](#cite:1056)
What a small firm must have: the sweep found no certification prescribed; DIU's brief asks for a CAGE code or UEI if applicable [1065](#cite:1065)

pending_changes.text: FAR-overhaul numbering: in the overhauled Part 35 [model deviation text](#term:class-deviation) the [BAA](#term:baa) provision sits at 35.102 under Subpart 35.1 ([Presolicitation](#term:presolicitation)), not 35.016; the technique "must only be used when meaningful proposals with varying technical/scientific approaches are reasonably expected". No date for the model text was visible, and it does not mention [CSOs](#term:cso) [1045](#cite:1045).

name: Broad Agency Announcement (FAR 35.016)
what: Under [FAR](#term:far) 35.016, broad agency announcements (BAAs) "may be used by agencies to fulfill their requirements for scientific study and experimentation directed toward advancing the state-of-the-art", and only when meaningful proposals with varying technical/scientific approaches can be reasonably anticipated [271](#cite:271). A BAA is for basic and applied research and development not related to a specific system or hardware requirement [1057](#cite:1057) [271](#cite:271).
who_for: Firms and institutions offering research and development approaches to an agency's stated research interest [271](#cite:271). The sweep found nothing specific to small firms prescribed in 35.016 [271](#cite:271).
how_it_works: The BAA describes the agency's research interest, the selection criteria and their relative importance, the proposal period, and submission instructions (35.016(b)) [271](#cite:271)
Publicized through the [Governmentwide point of entry](#term:sam-gov); "The notice must be published no less frequently than annually." (35.016(c)) [271](#cite:271)
Evaluated by peer or scientific review; written evaluation required; proposals need not be evaluated against each other (35.016(d)) [271](#cite:271)
Primary bases for selection are technical merit, importance to agency programs, and fund availability (35.016(e)) [271](#cite:271)
No separate subpart 5.2 [synopsis](#term:synopsis) for individual awards (35.016(f)) [271](#cite:271)
As DoD's comparison page puts it: budget activities 6.1–6.4; "Cannot be used for production"; must be funded with RDT&E funds; may result in FAR contracts or non-FAR agreements [1057](#cite:1057)
Relation to the CSO: "CSO procedures are similar to Broad Agency Announcement procedures, but CSOs are broader" [1056](#cite:1056)
A DARPA BAA Guide (Nov 2016) is listed in the [ARPA-H](#term:arpa-h) policy library; it was not read [1068](#cite:1068)

pending_changes.text: [Pub. L. 119-60](#term:ndaa) carries a section headed "Sec. 1845 [Facility clearance](#term:facility-clearance) acceleration for members of defense industrial consortiums"; only the heading was read [806](#cite:806).

[GAO](#term:gao) recommended in GAO-22-105357 that DoD maintain and regularly update a comprehensive list of DoD [consortia](#term:consortium) with active [OTA](#term:other-transaction) awards (recommendation 5); DoD agreed with the report's six recommendations, which the product page shows as three "Open – Partially Addressed" and three "Open" (status noted as of January 2025) [1119](#cite:1119) [1071](#cite:1071).

conflicts: The list lags the managers' own pages: the MITRE list does not show JDEC [1115](#cite:1115) vs [1137](#cite:1137); it shows MTEC under ATI and NSC as member-led, which ATI's and MTEC's own pages do not confirm [1115](#cite:1115) vs [1157](#cite:1157) [1179](#cite:1179).

Official status of the list: the MITRE page carries no statement of official status [1115](#cite:1115); the DoD notice naming it was read only on a commercial mirror because the SAM.gov original would not render [1116](#cite:1116) [1117](#cite:1117); no 2025 or 2026 notice was found.

Share of OT money through consortia differs by period and base: nearly two-thirds of prototype OTA dollars in FY2019–2021 [1071](#cite:1071); about half of prototype OTA obligations in FY2021–2024 [1121](#cite:1121); "roughly half of DOD's OT obligations are awarded to consortia." [1127](#cite:1127).

Manager compensation: 0.7% to 21.3% of obligated dollars on GAO's 12 OTAs [1119](#cite:1119); 1.55% to 6% of project value in the Inspector General's sample [1124](#cite:1124). Different samples and bases.

Secondary only: MITRE's explainer describes a consortium manager awarding agreements to member organizations, defines the form ("An OT Consortium is a relationship between a government sponsor and a collection of traditional and non-traditional vendors") and says "Many consortia do not award follow-on production activities." [1118](#cite:1118).

(Synthesis flagged by the sweep) A traditional contractor can take a consortium project by teaming with a nontraditional defense contractor that participates significantly or by paying a third of the cost; this is the sweep's reading of the statute and the NAC FAQ, not a statement in either [1029](#cite:1029) [1169](#cite:1169).
name: Consortium membership: join a consortium, respond to its requests
governing_text: 10 U.S.C. 4022 (prototype OTs; a transaction includes all individual prototype subprojects awarded under it to a consortium); each consortium's base agreement and membership agreement; DoD Other Transactions Guide, Version 2.0, Appendix F (not read)
what: For most OT consortia, "members pay dues to join the consortium and gain exclusive access to government opportunities" [1071](#cite:1071). DoD awards a [base OTA](#term:base-agreement) to a [consortium management organization](#term:consortium-manager); "[DOD](#term:department-of-war) selects the consortium member awardee and typically awards the project to the CMO.", which issues a sub-award to the member [1120](#cite:1120) [1119](#cite:1119). Consortia-based OTAs account for half of DoD's prototype OTA obligations, FY2021–FY2024 [1070](#cite:1070) [1121](#cite:1121).
who_for: Traditional and nontraditional firms alike: consortium pages say "Companies that are part of the US Defense Industrial base as well as new and emerging non-traditional defense contractors are encouraged to join" [1170](#cite:1170) [1192](#cite:1192). Membership is mostly nontraditional: 80% to 85% at the four consortia GAO examined [1121](#cite:1121); NSTXL states 83% non-traditional members [1138](#cite:1138); NAMC 70% [1228](#cite:1228); SOSSEC "Nearly 80% of the membership are non-traditional companies." [1233](#cite:1233); ATI says "80% of our members are small or emerging innovators" [1157](#cite:1157).
how_it_works: Find the consortium: MITRE's AiDA page lists 36 OT consortia grouped by sponsor (9 OSD-sponsored, 6 Air Force/Space Force, 10 Army, 8 Navy, 3 non-DoD), each with focus, sponsoring office, manager and URL; last updated 2025-09-22 [1115](#cite:1115). A DoD notice of 2024-04-24 (HQ0102240001), read only through a commercial mirror, points to that page as the [fiscal year](#term:fiscal-year) 2024 DoD consortia list maintained under Section 833 of [Public Law](#term:public-law) 116-283 [1116](#cite:1116) [1117](#cite:1117)

Join: one NSTXL membership covers every OTA NSTXL manages [1138](#cite:1138) [1141](#cite:1141); ATI consortia are joined one by one in three steps: find a consortium, apply, then access [solicitations](#term:solicitation) once accepted [1156](#cite:1156); CMG's C5 and CEED each take their own application [1220](#cite:1220) [1222](#cite:1222)

Documents commonly asked for: a signed Consortium Membership Agreement; a [UEI](#term:uei); an active [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) account; an active DD2345; a [CAGE code](#term:cage-code); for firms under foreign ownership, a FOCI mitigation plan or Export Compliance Acknowledgment Form [1160](#cite:1160) [1168](#cite:1168) [1185](#cite:1185) [1187](#cite:1187) [1201](#cite:1201)

Dues as posted run from nothing (NSTIC, RRPV, Cornerstone; DIBC in the first year) [1193](#cite:1193) [1215](#cite:1215) [1235](#cite:1235) [1191](#cite:1191), through $250 a year (MCDC, CWMD) [1185] [1187] and $500 a year (TReX II, VLC, C5, CEED, NAMC) [1160](#cite:1160) [1178](#cite:1178) [1220](#cite:1220) [1222](#cite:1222) [1229](#cite:1229), to $1,000 or $5,000 a year at MTEC [1180](#cite:1180) and up to $10,000 at NSTXL for corporate members with annual revenue of $100M+ [1138](#cite:1138); NAC charges a one-time $500 [1168](#cite:1168). Exact tables are in programs.yaml

Fees on awards: NSTIC assesses 0.05% of all awarded funding; AMTC 0.15%; DOTC and NEST 0.5% [1194](#cite:1194) [1169](#cite:1169) [1172](#cite:1172). C5 and CEED each assess "a small management and administrative fee, expressed as a fixed percentage" with no rate on the page [1220](#cite:1220) [1222](#cite:1222). NSTXL says "NSTXL is paid a management fee by the Government." and takes no percentage of the performer's invoice [1142](#cite:1142)

Requests: the sponsor issues a request to members through the manager (a Request for White Papers at C5 and DOTC, a Request for Solutions or Request for Prototype Proposal at NSTXL, a Request for Project Proposals at MTEC); members answer; the Government evaluates and selects; a full proposal follows for selected concepts [1224](#cite:1224) [1166](#cite:1166) [1143](#cite:1143) [1182](#cite:1182) [1227](#cite:1227)

Who may respond: "You must be a member of NSTXL to submit a response to any request." [1142](#cite:1142); NAMC says "These projects are all exclusive to NAMC—perks of the consortia" [1229](#cite:1229)

Who may look: S²MARTS requests are posted publicly while SpEC requests need membership and a DD2345 [1142](#cite:1142); DOTC's schedule is public but "To view complete solicitation information please visit the NAC Members Only site." [1166](#cite:1166); MTEC, NASC and NSTXL list solicitation titles or statuses without login [1182](#cite:1182) [1226](#cite:1226) [1143](#cite:1143)

The statutory condition is applied project by project: "DOTC, NEST, and AMTC solicitations require [NDC](#term:nontraditional-defense-contractor) participation or 1/3 [cost share](#term:cost-share) on each proposed effort." [1169](#cite:1169); the 2017 C5 base agreement requires one-third cost share unless an NDC participates to a significant extent or all significant participants are small businesses or NDCs [1224](#cite:1224); NSWC Crane briefed the same condition for S²MARTS [1152](#cite:1152)
"A transaction includes all individual prototype subprojects awarded under the transaction to a consortium of United States industry and academic institutions." [1029](#cite:1029)

Award: under the 2017 C5 base agreement a bilateral modification obligates project funding, a Technical Direction Letter authorizes work, and the manager issues a Project Agreement to the selected member [1224](#cite:1224); at NSTXL agreement finalization takes about 3–5 business days after selection notice [1142](#cite:1142)

Registration: "each member serving as the primary performer on an award must obtain a Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) from SAM." [1049](#cite:1049); the [Inspector General](#term:dod-ig) found in 2021 that there was no DoD requirement for consortium members to register in SAM [1124](#cite:1124)

Time to award as managers state it: NSTXL "just over 100 days" on average [1144](#cite:1144); SpEC reports one request-to-award in under 8 months [1147](#cite:1147); UTIC issues requests for prototype proposals twice a year [1198](#cite:1198); DOTC releases a Request for White Papers each month [1166](#cite:1166)

Why agencies use consortia, per officials GAO interviewed: a ready pool of vendors including nontraditional ones; government–industry collaboration before solicitation; administrative support through a single point of contact; faster execution using standard templates [1119](#cite:1119). NSWC Crane's reasons for one broad consortium: avoid a proliferation of OTAs and "Limit burden to small vendors, no need to join several consortia" [1152](#cite:1152)

Criticisms on record, dues and overlap: "Officials from one company told us their firm has joined 20 different consortia and pays about $30,000 a year in membership dues."; several consortia cover the same technology areas; a DARPA official said dues may exclude innovative companies [1119](#cite:1119)

Criticisms on record, manager pay: consortium management organization compensation ranged from 0.7% to 21.3% of obligated dollars on 12 OTAs GAO reviewed, at least $332 million in FY2019–2021, paid by seven methods [1119](#cite:1119); the Inspector General found fees of 1.55% to 6% of project value and no guidance for negotiating them [1124](#cite:1124) [1123](#cite:1123)

Criticisms on record, competition: "DoD contracting personnel did not always compete base OTs to the maximum extent practicable" [1124](#cite:1124); [CRS](#term:crs) records the argument that consortia "reduce competition, since only members of the consortium under contract can participate." alongside GAO's finding that members gain exclusive access [1079](#cite:1079) [1071](#cite:1071)

What a small firm must have: membership in the consortium that carries the sponsor's work; for most defense consortia read, a DD2345; a UEI from SAM to be primary performer [1160](#cite:1160) [1168](#cite:1168) [1196](#cite:1196) [1049](#cite:1049)

name: NASA Space Act Agreement (51 U.S.C. 20113(e))
governing_text: 51 U.S.C. 20113(e); NASA Partnerships Guide, NAII 1050-3D (original 2016-12-21; last updated 2026-04-07)
what: [NASA](#term:agency-abbreviations) may enter into and perform contracts, leases, [cooperative agreements](#term:grant), or [other transactions](#term:other-transaction) as necessary, on terms it deems appropriate [1088](#cite:1088); NASA's Partnerships Guide cites 51 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 20113(e) as the Other Transactions Authority of the Space Act [1089](#cite:1089). The same subsection directs that, to the maximum extent practicable, these be allocated "in a manner which will enable small-business concerns to participate equitably and proportionately in the conduct of the work of the Administration" [1088](#cite:1088).
who_for: Partners of NASA; a funded agreement goes to a domestic partner [1089](#cite:1089).
how_it_works: Three kinds. Reimbursable: the partner reimburses NASA's costs. Nonreimbursable: each party bears its own costs with no exchange of funds. Funded: NASA transfers appropriated funds to a domestic partner and does not take ownership of deliverables as it would under a procurement contract [1089](#cite:1089)

Funded agreements may be used only "when the Agency cannot accomplish its objectives through the use of a procurement contract, grant, or cooperative agreement, and only after [full and open competition](#term:full-and-open-competition)" [1089](#cite:1089)
The authority is exercised without regard to 31 U.S.C. 3324(a) and (b) [1088](#cite:1088)
Scale (dated): NASA used about 2,220 other transaction agreements in 2010 and about 3,220 in 2014 [1073](#cite:1073)

conflicts: "Non-traditional" differs by agency: DOE's guide uses no Federal prime award for at least five years [1093](#cite:1093); DoD's 10 U.S.C. 3014 uses no DoD contract or subcontract under full cost accounting standards coverage in the prior year [1032](#cite:1032).
Expiry: the fetch tool reported a "September 30, 2030" date in 42 U.S.C. 7256(g) without clear context [1092](#cite:1092); DOE's guide states no expiration [1093](#cite:1093). Unresolved.
name: DOE other transaction (42 U.S.C. 7256)
governing_text: 42 U.S.C. 7256(a) and (g); Energy Policy Act of 2005, sections 988 and 1007; 2 CFR Part 930 (Technology Investment Agreements issued on or after January 3, 2025; formerly 10 CFR 603); DOE Guide to Other Transactions (August 2023)
what: The Secretary of Energy "may exercise the same authority to enter into transactions (other than contracts, [cooperative agreements](#term:grant), and grants), subject to the same terms and conditions" as the Secretary of Defense under 10 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 2371 [now 4021], other than subsections (b) and (f) [1092](#cite:1092). [DOE](#term:agency-abbreviations)'s guide distinguishes the general authority in section 7256(a) from the R&D authority in section 7256(g) [1093](#cite:1093). DOE names the DOE Organization Act, 42 U.S.C. 7256, and the Energy Policy Act of 2005 as the authority [1094](#cite:1094).
who_for: Research and development partners of DOE; DOE's guide defines non-traditional contractors as entities that have not received a Federal prime award for at least five years [1093](#cite:1093). Unsolicited proposals go to the National Energy Technology Laboratory [1094](#cite:1094).
how_it_works: Conditions in the statute: competitive, merit-based selection procedures as practicable; a written determination that a standard contract, grant or cooperative agreement is not feasible or appropriate; delegable only to a presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed officer [1092](#cite:1092)

Approval: section 7256(g) agreements need approval by a Senate-confirmed officer with delegated authority; all [OTs](#term:other-transaction) go through Office of Acquisition Management business clearance and Senior Procurement Executive approval [1093](#cite:1093)

[Cost share](#term:cost-share): the EPAct section 1007 standard is that Government funds do not exceed the total from other parties; EPAct section 988 allows reduction or elimination for applied R&D [1093](#cite:1093)

Patents: without Bayh-Dole, title to inventions would vest in DOE under its title-vesting statutes unless the agreement provides otherwise; section 7256(g) allows negotiation of patent and [data rights](#term:sbir-data-rights) [1093](#cite:1093)
"U.S. manufacturing [clauses](#term:clause-numbering) should almost always be included to the extent feasible and practicable" [1093](#cite:1093)

[Consortia](#term:consortium): "Consortium arrangements are commercial agreements and DOE is not party to the consortium"; a consortium may be run by a lead member or by a [consortium manager](#term:consortium-manager) [1093](#cite:1093)
Technology Investment Agreements are governed by 2 [CFR](#term:cfr) Part 930 for agreements issued on or after January 3, 2025, replacing 10 CFR 603 [1094](#cite:1094)

[ARPA-E](#term:arpa-e), inside DOE, has its own award authority: "the Director may provide awards in the form of grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, cash prizes, and other transactions" (42 U.S.C. 16538(f)); no public ARPA-E OT guide was found [1100](#cite:1100)

name: FAA other transaction (49 U.S.C. 106(l)(6))

what: The [FAA](#term:agency-abbreviations) Administrator may enter into and perform "such contracts, leases, [cooperative agreements](#term:grant), or [other transactions](#term:other-transaction) as may be necessary to carry out the functions of the Administrator and the Administration" [1101](#cite:1101). name: NIH other transaction (42 U.S.C. 282(n))
governing_text: 42 U.S.C. 282(n) (PHS Act section 402(n)); PHS Act section 421(b)(3) (NHLBI) and section 480(e)(3)(C) (NCATS); NIH "Other Transactions" (OT) Policy Guide (May 22, 2017)
what: The [NIH](#term:agency-abbreviations) Director may approve requests by institutes and centers "to engage in transactions other than a contract, [grant](#term:grant), or cooperative agreement" for projects that carry out the Precision Medicine Initiative; Common Fund research, limited to 50 percent of Common Fund amounts available for that purpose in a [fiscal year](#term:fiscal-year); or high impact cutting-edge research or research urgently required to respond to a public health threat [1097](#cite:1097). NIH describes an [OT](#term:other-transaction) as "a unique type of legal instrument other than a contract, grant, or cooperative agreement" [1098](#cite:1098).
who_for: NIH says OTs are used to reach nontraditional recipients such as patient advocacy organizations, pharmaceutical companies and foreign entities [1098](#cite:1098). Its 2017 policy guide names small businesses, patient advocacy organizations, educational institutions, pharmaceutical companies, foreign entities, [consortia](#term:consortium), nonprofits and individuals as possible partners [1099](#cite:1099).
how_it_works: Authorities NIH names: PHS Act section 402(n) (NIH Director); section 421(b)(3) (NHLBI); section 480(e)(3)(C) (NCATS, capped at 20 percent of annual appropriations) [1098](#cite:1098)
Applications go through eRA ASSIST under each opportunity announcement [1098](#cite:1098)

IP: "Flexibility in the negotiation of IP rights is one of the rationales for using an OT."; [Agreements Officers](#term:contracting-officer) can negotiate IP terms that differ from other funding instruments [1099](#cite:1099)
The policy guide's Appendix 1 lists authorities and Appendix 2 lists laws that may not apply, including CICA and the [Contract Disputes Act](#term:contract-disputes-act) [1099](#cite:1099)

name: ARPA-H other transaction (42 U.S.C. 290c)
governing_text: 42 U.S.C. 290c(g)(1)(D) and (g)(2); 42 U.S.C. 247d-7e(a)(3) (definition of other transactions)
what: [ARPA-H](#term:arpa-h) may enter into [other transactions](#term:other-transaction), as defined by 42 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 247d-7e(a)(3), subject to 290c(g)(2) [1096](#cite:1096). who_for: Performers of ARPA-H programs; resource sharing depends on the authority, and ARPA-H and several others are not required to use it [1067](#cite:1067).
how_it_works: "To the maximum extent practicable, competitive procedures shall be used when entering into other transactions under this section." [1096](#cite:1096)
A program manager's written request and the Director's approval are required; annual report [1096](#cite:1096)
CICA does not apply; most OT authorities require competitive procedures to the maximum extent practicable [1067](#cite:1067)
IP: "OTs allow for complete flexibility and freedom in negotiating rights" [1066](#cite:1066)

[Protests](#term:bid-protest): "OTs can be protested, but what can be protested and where protests must be filed is more complicated and less established"; [GAO](#term:gao) has limited jurisdiction [1067](#cite:1067)

Public guidance: ARPA-H's Other Transaction Community pages (FAQs; policies and guidance from several agencies; legal and protest decisions) and a cross-government OT training deck dated 2025-06-25 [1067](#cite:1067) [1068](#cite:1068) [1069](#cite:1069) [1066](#cite:1066)

[BARDA](#term:barda), also in [HHS](#term:agency-abbreviations), holds the underlying authority at 42 U.S.C. 247d-7e(c)(5): competitive procedures to the maximum extent practicable, and a written determination by the Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources for projects expected to cost HHS more than $100,000,000; no public BARDA OT guide was found [1095](#cite:1095).
